Lin and Mesnager discovered a new class of optimal difference sets, which has practical applications in increasing the nonlinearity of complete vectorial Boolean mappings. This work aims to extend the definition of difference sets to difference set like sequences and presents three new types. The proposed sets have distinct differences, leading to lower nonlinearity when using the first type and distinct differences when using the second type. The third type features distinct differences when considering its modified form. The nonlinearity associated with the third type is explored in detail, and it is demonstrated that its minimum is achieved at the four-element difference set, also resulting in a recovery of the minimum nonlinearity of APN functions from difference sets. Additionally, it is found that the distinct differences in the fifth type can be obtained from difference sets, leading to new examples of vectorial Boolean mappings with a nonlinearity of 2^m-2^{m/2}-2^{(m+1)/2}.

Binary matrices that alternate in rows and columns can be margined consistently, 
meaning their row and column sums follow an alternating pattern. The set of all such 
matrices, denoted as $\mathcal{M}$, contains those with given marginal values. Given the relevance of this set in various applications such as statistical modeling, image processing, and network analysis, efficiently sampling from $\mathcal{M}$ is a crucial research area. This paper presents an algorithm for uniformly generating single constant margin binary arrays, contributing to the larger goal of sampling from the given set.

Intense LHC data examination requires precise modification of parton distribution functions to pinpoint the source of any discrepancy between theoretical predictions and experimental findings. A new computational framework, PDF4LHC, is responsible for establishing adjusted PDF models that account for such uncertainties. The PDF4LHC framework operates in two stages: initially, individual PDF sets are derived from specific theoretical approaches and validated against relevant LHC measurements; subsequently, these sets are combined within the framework to create an ensemble of predictions and assign weights to each set based on their reliability in describing observed phenomena. The pdfmod tool has been developed to integrate updates into existing PDF sets, incorporating modified cross-section predictions where direct measurements are unavailable. The pdfmod tool and selected PDF sets will be made accessible to the community through public download starting from July 2018 on the PDF4LHC Framework website, along with the latest status reports and plans for future developments and updates.

This document serves as the first update to ELKI, a comprehensive data mining toolkit, highlighting its core functionalities, design approach and offering an extensive open-source library for data quality assessment. ELKI integrates a vast collection of algorithms from diverse design methodologies - encompassing unsupervised, supervised, semi-supervised, and unsupervised learning techniques - along with their variants. The primary focus, however, lies on density-based data mining, particularly clustering, anomaly detection, and near-duplicate detection methodologies. The toolset is presented in the context of a comprehensive framework for metric space data processing. The framework's simplicity, combined with its robust feature extraction capabilities, enables efficient metric space data processing. The toolkit is written in the Java programming language, known for its extensive library support and cross-platform compatibility. The toolset is complemented by a vast collection of test datasets, known as data markets, which facilitate reproducible and open-access experimental settings. In addition to showcasing the toolset's capabilities, this document also discusses the concept of data markets - promoting open-access data analysis through transparent and accessible methodologies.

A new technique has been developed to rapidly create optical frequency grids. 
This innovative method involves lock-in-loop control of laser frequency using a microresonator, and when pulsed power is applied, it generates a cascade of Stokes and anti-Stokes frequency peaks. It eliminates the limitations of previous techniques, allowing for a wider frequency range and better resolution. It also has a simpler design and lower cost compared to alternative methods.

We demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of a stochastic subgroup of a non-elemental acylindrically hyperbolic group, which is randomly generated by two elements and proves to be the group's only proper stochastic subgroup.

This study delves into the theoretical underpinnings of generalization in binary weight neural networks from the perspective of the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK). Through this analysis, distinct characteristics of the binary NTK (bNTK) are identified and it is demonstrated that bNTK exhibits a low-rank structure and isotropic properties. These discoveries lead to the formulation of generalization bounds for classification and regression tasks, revealing that the unique rank and symmetry attributes of bNTK contribute to its superior generalization capabilities. In addition, the influence of different activation functions on generalization is examined, with the findings indicating that symmetric activation functions are optimal for binary networks and that non-strict monotonicity is crucial for achieving good generalization in the ResNet architecture. Building on the theoretical framework established, the study's principles are utilized to guide binary neural network quantization strategies to further improve generalization performance.

We employ the generalized entropy formula to identify Extreme Surface configurations in quantum gravity theories and demonstrate their relationship with boundary entropy patterns. Specifically, the patterns of Entanglement Renormalization Theory emerge naturally from the patterns of Extremal Entanglement Structure. Furthermore, the difference between von Neumann entanglement entropies on the largest and smallest boundaries of an entanglement wedge is equal to the von Neumann entanglement entropy across the extremal surface itself. This finding is verified through direct calculation in a specific Luttinger liquid model. Additionally, the relationship of extremal surfaces to black hole entropy in loop quantum gravity is explored, and the presence of boundary corrections to the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy in Luttinger liquid models is accounted for.

We introduce a new general framework to determine the count of resolvable lattice models,
an innovative method that includes previously established methods as special cases.
Our approach allows us to derive a formula that gives the total count of resolvable models
of any type and size in any given dimension. Utilizing this formula, we are able to
reproduce known results and discover new formulas for the number of geometric models
and algebraic structures of various dimensions.

This research focuses on developing and analyzing certain stabilization techniques for a class of non-linear iterative algorithms used in compressed sensing. These stabilization techniques can improve the stability and convergence of iterative methods by constraining solutions within a predetermined bounded area. Our investigation demonstrates that when certain compressed sensing models utilize iterative methods with stabilization techniques, the constrained solutions can be represented as the output of a non-expansive operator. Furthermore, under specific conditions, we are able to prove the convergence of these constrained solutions.

We examine how to combine images with varying point spread functions (PSFs), considering cases where PSFs are uniform or vary across the image, and we explore the challenges and implications of combining images with differing PSFs. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the effective PSF of a combined image can deviate significantly from the average PSF, even comprising elements that exceed the brightest star's flux by an order of magnitude. This phenomenon is relevant to techniques such as deconvolution, angular differential photometry, and similar methods that aim to correct for PSF effects.

We introduce new probabilistic models comprising both Euclidean and Choquet-Davidian surfaces, associated with an ensemble of log-correlated random points. These models are seamlessly connected to established theory of planar Brownian motion through a multipoint coupling approach. Specifically, we establish that the law of our surface is equivalent to the conditional law of the Gaussian free field given these points, with Brownian clusters serving as their complementary component.

For three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations in a periodic space, we consider solutions with smooth, zero-average initial velocities and constant pressures, surrounded by incompressible incompressible forces with smooth averages. We provide theoretical evaluations of the velocity and periodic solution of the Navier-Stokes equations, along with their derivatives up to the specified order, of the pressure, and the averages of the external forces, of the solutions norms of the corresponding spaces.

This research presents a method for verifying the results of quantum computations within linear time, based on the assumption that verification of individual intermediate states also yields the final result's verification, thus allowing a quadratic reduction in space usage, from n^2 to n^2/log^2(n). We achieve this by introducing the concept of "qrels", a space-efficient format for storing quantum circuit evaluations, enabling related quantities to be computed recursively and similarly. It is shown that any evaluation can be represented as a qrel in polylog(n) space, and that the verification of the final result can be achieved by linear time operations, including the use of a working memory buffer of size polylog(n). We extend this framework to verify quantum circuit outputs with m bits as log^2(m) * polylog(n), and demonstrate the applicability of this method to two specific algorithms: Grover's algorithm and the Euclidean GCD.

Achieving diversity and realism in generating synthetic data, such as images, poses a significant challenge to researchers working on generative modeling. A promising generative representation, implicit neural networks, has shown great potential in reconstructing complex functions, surfaces, and volumes. However, generating diverse shapes from learned latent representations and encoding detailed geometries with learned weights has historically been difficult. To overcome these obstacles, we have developed a novel framework that utilizes implicit neural representation (INR) as a generative model for creating diverse and realistic shapes. By leveraging an implicit surface model trained on shape data and employing random labels, we can generate diverse shapes without requiring discrete latent variables. Furthermore, we randomize the training of our model, eliminating the need for weight-based geometric interpretation. Our approach yields high-quality, diverse generations of complex and irregular shapes. A thorough evaluation of our model and ablation studies are provided.

We performed simple experiments to test the capabilities of different self-organizing map topologies in a grid world using a reward-based learning approach. The experiments revealed that the grid topology effectively supports reinforcement learning for navigating straightforward environments, whereas the hexagonal topology is suitable for more complex settings with obstacles, and the triangular topology works well in even more intricate environments with obstacles and random reward patterns. Furthermore, we found that the learning process using the hexagonal and triangular topologies often involves initial fluctuations, potentially posing a challenge in real-time applications, and even a potential risk of unintended consequences during the learning process.

The standard 'Metropolis' algorithm is a widely used tool for sampling data from a specified probability distribution and generating Markov chains, such as the Ising model, which is notoriously difficult to simulate due to the trapping of exploratory steps in local minima. To overcome this challenge, modifications of the update rule, like tunneling methods, have been developed, but they often introduce additional computational overhead. Our research presents a novel application of hard-sphere dynamics, specifically in the context of the Ising model, to demonstrate a simpler method that avoids this complexity. Our work extends previous studies on tunneling methods, drawing parallels between standard and modified update rules, as well as between different types of modifications. We found that a specific hard-sphere dynamics method, the 'Boltzmann' algorithm, effectively simulates the Ising model, outperforming the traditional Metropolis method.

The challenge of locating sound sources in complex environments with multiple obstacles is extremely complex due to significant variations in acoustic cues. To overcome this limitation, we propose using microphone array outputs as input, allowing our model to exploit modified acoustic information. To do so, we implement a data enhancement technique by rotating the microphone array, resulting in multiple modified views, and feed it to a network, leading to a 3D audio event detection model. This approach is similar to 2D extended deep networks and yields improved performance. Notably, our proposed model, although simple in design, outperforms current state-of-the-art 3D sound event localization and identification models, even with limited microphone array baselines.

As wireless communication systems reach their limits, researchers are exploring innovative solutions to surpass conventional techniques, with concurrent transmission emerging as a promising approach. By utilizing superposition, CT enables the integration of multiple services and technologies within a single frequency, time, and space, optimizing existing systems rather than building from scratch. Enchantment by its versatility and efficiency, CT-based wireless systems aim to optimize resources, enhance system capacity, and prepare for 6G's envisioned capabilities. This review explores the potential of CT, offering insights into its unique features, underlying principles, and promising applications, accompanied by a comprehensive bibliography to inspire further innovation in this field.

We suggest a signal detection approach rooted in the geometric properties of spectrogram slices. By segmenting the spectrogram into equal-sized grids, we obtain a collection of maximum intensities that follow an exponential distribution with a grid-dependent parameter. This paper derives the distribution of grid sizes and demonstrates the relationship between the maximum intensity and the grid parameter, leading to a simplified evaluation method based on the smallest grid parameter value. This approach is equivalent to traditional detection techniques, such as those using coherent energy or matched energy, but with a crucial distinction: our method applies to spectrograms, not the raw signal. This relationship enables us to define detection rules for a variety of signal evaluation methods and settings, providing a unified framework for signal detection that works across different scenarios and includes both coherent and incoherent, as well Bayesian approaches.

Detecting the transportation of localized wavepackets and areas of synchronization in networks of neurons, known as chimeras, is hindered by developing techniques that are not fully effective due to their vulnerability to dynamical systems' complexities. Moreover, the majority of previously established approaches are specifically tailored to symmetric, non-interactive networks without perturbations, limiting their applicability. In our research, we have created a innovative, universal approach to identify and monitor the spread of wavepackets and synchronized regions in larger, perturbed networks, using a simulation of a 5000-neuron network. Our novel methodology employs the correlation dimension's finite size scaling analysis to identify homogeneous areas within a network, applying this concept to a ring of coupled Hindmarsh-Rose neurons. Our findings demonstrate that this methodology can effectively distinguish between synchronized regions and traveling wavepackets in networks, and are confirmed by comparisons with results from mean-field analysis. Our work specifically shows that the correlation dimension's finite size scaling analysis can be used to identify and differentiate between synchronized regions and traveling wavepackets in networks, and by extension, may offer a promising alternative for studying brain dynamics through its potential connection to brain imaging techniques.

A novel execution method is presented for the $N$-body code REBOUND and its MJIT derived implementation, allowing users to apply forces in an randomized manner. This execution method facilitates the simulation of unstated forces such as drag or damping on particles, and can simulate multiple additional particles representing unresolved masses or both, enabling the simulation of unified forces such as Wangman gravity. By default, this execution method selects "thread safety" for consistency across users, however, user may opt to select "lock-free" for enhanced performance at the cost of potentially varying results among different users. To illustrate the randomized force simulation, two examples are provided - one demonstrating the formation and evolution of a disk around a central astromass due to the presence of particles and opposing forces such as drag, and the other showing the simulation of supermassive black holes utilizing the REBOUND PJIT implementation and the MJIT code for consistency across platforms.

The quantum Eckhardt filter marks one of the first instances of online feedback regulation being applied to quantum systems. We've derived a Markovian evolution equation that describes the joint dynamics of an observed quantum system and the estimator's state. This equation, analogous to the quantum Liouville-Lindblad equation, incorporates an additional term that accounts for the feedback regulation process. Notably, this regulation can be viewed as a controlled interaction regulated by the estimator, enabling access to new functionalities in quantum technologies. To illustrate the potential applications of the Eckhardt filter, we examine a scenario where it enables the generation of entanglement between remapping memories of an otherwise unentangled pair of photons.

This research builds upon the findings of Loeb and Krug on the properties of alternating sequences of discs in two dimensions with varying blocked areas, where the blocked areas represent masses within a one-dimensional channel of unit length and are arranged in a specified order, where masses within non-consecutive blocked areas may overlap. We derive a closed-form expression for the smallest blocked disc with area zero, provided its center is centered, in the scenario where the masses follow a pattern of $a_1-a_2-a_1-a_2-a_1$, discovering a zero-crossing phenomenon of the function $R(x)$, where $x$ represents the centered disc with area zero, occurring at the harmonic mean of $a_1$ and $a_2$. We generalize the results to a sequence of parameters $a_1-a_2-a_1-a_2-a_1\ldots$ and examine the behavior of the alternating disc function $R(x)$, analyzing the set of zeroes of $R(x)$, where the parameter $x$ is also considered, under various conditions of the masses $a_i$. We also study the behavior of the parameters $x_0$ and $R(x_0)$, where $R(x_0)$ tends to zero, in the scenario where the masses $a_i$ tend to zero, where the masses $a_i$ represent the blocked areas of the discs, in the blocked disc problem, where the smallest disc with area zero

El Ni\~no--Southern Oscillation impacts global weather, particularly affecting rainfall in regions heavily dependent on seasonal storms. Recent studies emphasize the importance of examining El Ni\~no's multiple varieties to accurately understand their effects on extreme climate events. We conducted the first detailed investigation into how different varieties of El Ni\~no influence patterns of very low and high seasonal rainfall worldwide. Our analysis, which involved screening storm tracks using satellite data from 1997 to 2017, reveals that not all El Ni\~no events have the same impact on storm activity. El Ni\~no–like conditions associated with very low rainfall are found to be linked to reduced precipitation in the Americas and Oceania, but our results show that not all varieties of El Ni\~no produce the same level of reduction. El Ni\~no events associated with very low rainfall are found to be linked to reduced precipitation in the Americas and Oceania, but our results show that not all varieties of El Ni\~no produce the same level of reduction.

Recent studies have revealed numerous small satellite galaxies within the Local Group containing massive black holes with masses exceeding 10,000 suns. The evolution of these galaxies hints that their black holes might have formed as isolated entities prior to the galaxy's emergence. Although no definitive proof exists yet, the ancestors of these satellites may be detectable through observations of their present-day structures. Theoretical models suggest that the presence of specific morphological features in these satellites - such as off-center stellar distributions or mass variations - could be attributed to past interactions between the black holes and stars. We investigated the potential signs of such interactions in Leo I, discovering that its mass distribution does not follow expected trends. The mass enclosed within a given radius shows an unusual upturn at a certain point, which could be attributed to either the influence of a recent byproduct of a Leo I satellite interaction or a more ancient interaction affecting the galaxy's structure. The study of Leo I's structure is a key step in understanding the role of black holes in the evolution of small galaxies.

In a three-dimensional multi-orbital Kagome structure, we demonstrate the presence of adverse magnetoresistance under specific conditions, such as when all Kagome symmetry orbits are occupied by electrons. This phenomenon, also observed in the half-filled single-band cubic perovskite, arises from the anti-localization to localization transition of electrons in response to a magnetic field aligned with the crystal lattice. Although the adverse magnetoresistance typically manifests in alloys with strong disorder and localized electrons, we found that this effect can also manifest in coherent multi-orbital Kagome systems where the flat band induced instability results in strong correlations and localized states induced by the magnetic field alignment.

An integrated analysis of genome-wide association studies and gene regulatory networks across 18 traits revealed 8,486 genes potentially linked to specific characteristics. By comparing the enrichment of observed genes within these studies to those identified at random, researchers discovered significant parallels between the studies, which also revealed distinct patterns of regulatory activity across different traits. This analysis yielded over 1,000 gene targets as candidates for functioning within the pathways defined by the network, two of which were experimentally confirmed as essential to the traits. These findings support the development of a data-driven approach to genomic network analysis, which may be utilized to discover and validate new associations between genes and characteristics.

A particular type of combinatorial design, a flag-transitive symmetric block configuration, involves a set with a group acting upon it. This group must satisfy two conditions, one related to the configuration's points and the other regarding its lines. We've identified all such configurations, particularly those with prime or square-prime parameters, with specific restrictions on the configuration's parameters and a large prime number involved. Our work also generalizes previous findings on transversal designs.

For confined helium-like atoms, the effects of Coulomb interaction are examined, 
initially ignoring these effects and representing the influence of non-coulombian 
parts with entropy measures that adhere to Schrodinger's equation. Next, incorporating 
the Coulomb interaction, information entropies are calculated using helium mass 
and reduced masses for other atomic masses. Furthermore, for confined helium-like 
atoms, the Coulomb effects have been found to shift the energies and influence 
the behaviors of the entropies.

Our analysis of the Cassini radio timing data reveals a comprehensive test of gravity in the Solar System's lower and outer regions. Employing a parameterized post-Newtonian framework that incorporates PN parameters $\beta$ and $\gamma$ to characterize deviations from general relativity, our findings confirm that a rigorous statistical assessment, utilizing the Bayesian approach, strongly supports Einstein's gravity over its alternatives. Notably, our data precisely constrains the difference between the $\beta$ and $\gamma$ parameters to be within approximately 6e-5. Our research signifies the most accurate large-scale gravity test to date and proposes a novel, statistically sound methodology for evaluating gravitational theories, further validating the principle of unique relativity.

Multiplicative proofs serve as a valuable tool for model checking typed $\lambda$-calculi and type systems thanks to their recursive multiplicative removal and cut-removal capabilities, which directly translate to $\beta\eta$-reduction and graph reduction, respectively. However, the application of these capabilities in general type systems is hindered by the presence of exponential multiplicity. This work proposes the development of tailored removal and cut-removal strategies specifically designed for multiplicative linear logic, applicable to type systems featuring both linear and exponential resources. These strategies are illustrated through their implementation in the multiplicative type system derived from the lambda calculus $!\lambda$.

Predicting the simultaneous progression of time-series sequences from different domains is crucial for predicting synchronized events. Traditional predictive methods like dynamic time warping have limitations, particularly when dealing with long time-series sequences and real-time applications. A novel approach is presented that leverages condition state space mapping and cross recurrence plots to forecast synchronization in target time-series data. Using this method, time-series sequences are transformed into symbolic representations of their dynamic behavior. A machine learning model is then employed to anticipate the symbolic representation of the next state in the target sequence. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through its ability to forecast the synchronization of ankle joint motion patterns between healthy and cerebral palsy patients.

To analyze the impact of momentum on properties related to electrons, vibrations, and their interactions, researchers developed a model incorporating constraints from the Lyddane-Sachs-Todd relations and minimum momentum constraints within a lattice structure. This theoretical framework revealed the emergence of new modes of interaction known as sonic photons, which possess unique characteristics of acoustic phonons, such as a specific relationship between frequency and momentum, while exhibiting nonlinearity at higher momentum levels. Simulations of the interaction between electrons and these sonic photons, which include both dynamic aspects and vacuum forces, have shown a specific relationship between the interaction strength and the momentum, which contrasts with the expected behavior associated with acoustic phonons. Additionally, simulations of the coupling between spins and sonic photons, which consider the interaction between the orientation of photons and the direction of momentum, demonstrated the possibility of vacuum forces of a dipole type, which can be expressed as a function of the inverse of the fourth power of the momentum. These findings suggest the potential for new types of devices, such as phonon lasers, that operate based on the principles of momentum and the behavior of sonic photons.

Click-through rate (CTR) is a key metric for assessing online promotion efficacy, but predicting CTR for novel promotions is a significant challenge. Traditional CTR forecasting approaches based on historical data fail to account for the introduction of new promotions. In contrast, we propose material CTR MCTR, which enhances CTR predictions for new promotions by identifying and leveraging visual similarities among promotions sharing the same underlying material. Instead of analyzing entire promotions, MCTR focuses on constituent materials such as images, colors, and shapes, and represents them using graph-based methods. The material representations are then used to construct node types in a structured graph, which is further enhanced with node features. The proposed architecture utilizes graph neural networks to propagate node features and identify visual similarities among promotions, the results of which are applied to material cTR for more accurate CTR predictions. Notably, there are no existing methods that utilize visual information for CTR forecasting, and experimental findings confirm the effectiveness of our proposed approach.

This document introduces a set of technical enhancements to the definition of cardinality constraints, to the algorithms for generating possible system behaviors, and to the methods for verifying possible system behaviors, all within the framework of the axiomatic semantics described in the literature. The document builds upon the foundational semantics outlined in the comprehensive book and the previous technical reports providing outlines for the algorithms and verification techniques. The document specifically focuses on consistency and liveness verification algorithms and techniques.

Wildfires are a significant source of global air pollution, producing toxic aerosols such as PM2.5 and black carbon, which pose a threat to public health and the environment. Although wildfires can be monitored using various satellite systems, accurately predicting Wildfire Aerosol Mechanism Patterns (WAMP) remains a difficult task. To address this challenge, this study develops a theoretical framework that integrates data from multiple Geostationary Satellites (GEO-SAT) to create a unified analysis of WAMP, taking into account the physical processes of fire and the observations of atmospheric pollutants. By combining data from GEO-SAT satellites and the advantages of machine learning, this model provides a accurate and real-time prediction of WAMP, providing valuable insights for wildfire monitoring and air quality assessment.

In this study, we explore the concept of tracking privacy for discrete locations, measuring it as the maximum gain an adversary could achieve by knowing a user's exact location versus a rounded, bunched version of it. To effectively prevent tracking, randomized strategies like the Smallest Enclosing Ball and Discrete McShane's strategies are utilized. However, these methods can be limiting due to their strict requirements. Here, we relax the conditions for preventing tracking by accepting that an adversary should not expect to not track, rather than expecting not to track. By doing so, our approach enables the development of new, more flexible anti-tracking protocols for a variety of location distributions.

Investigating the human brain at rest is a crucial area of functional neuroimaging. This approach allows researchers to analyze spontaneous brain activity patterns, which can be measured using resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI). By quantifying brain signal strength, we can correlate brain regions, identify individual differences, and track changes. We developed a new statistical method to evaluate the reliability of resting-state connectivity, along with a corresponding prediction accuracy framework. This was applied across multiple large-scale datasets of healthy subjects and patients with schizophrenia, assessing the reliability of connecting specific brain areas. Our results indicate that certain connectivity measures have a sufficient level of precision for meaningful scientific investigation. Moreover, we found that the prediction precision of these measures can vary based on the individual, the specific brain area, and the scan conditions, but it can also be consistent, which is a positive sign for conducting large-scale studies using rs-fMRI.

In the context of complex network structures, we denoted the local degradability in terms of curvature and examined whether it influences heat diffusion within the network from aPpoca et al. (2020). Building upon this concept, we introduced a heat source with non-uniform distribution in the network and investigated its implications. We then investigated under what circumstances the equilibrium heat density within the network would adhere to a specified probability distribution. To achieve this goal, we developed a novel geometric characterization of the networks that accommodates a wide range of discrete structures while maintaining the specified probability distribution in steady-state thermal equilibrium. Finally, we provided examples of two-dimensional grid-like and free branching networks with uniform distribution and demonstrated that the proposed methods can be applied to assess network security by comparing their structural properties with those of their unattacked states.

Recent advancements in pre-trained models have made natural language processing more accessible, and research on code-mixed languages is gaining momentum. However, existing neural models are unable to leverage contextual information or positional relationships between words, and require extensive training resources. This paper presents a groundbreaking approach that overcomes these limitations by integrating position-encoded embeddings with a proposed dynamic representation for words across different languages within code-mixed sentences. Experimental results on the GIGABHAI and UDDN datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our model in identifying code-mixed Hindi-English, outperforming the best pre-trained and feature-based models, while also reducing training requirements compared to the pre-trained models. The source code and dataset are available at https://github.com/krishnatej99/PESTO.

The high-pressure superconductivity of hydrogen-based materials like H$_3$S has been extensively studied using first-principles calculations. By applying numerical data from quantum-mechanical atomistic simulations, researchers found that introducing larger atoms like Se into S in H$_2$Se impacts the density of states at the Fermi level and the isotopic dependency of critical temperatures in metal chalcogenides. Assuming this pattern holds for isotopic behavior and the application of Born-Carboville lattice dynamics, similar trends with isotope changes can be predicted for other materials. Applying this logic to the superconducting hydrogen sulfide H$_3$S, with its high-pressure superconducting properties known to be around 200 K, theoretical analysis suggests the critical pressure for T$_c$ = 200 K is 247 GPa. Furthermore, the role of electron-phonon interaction in this range is also analyzed and found the electron-phonon coupling constant is approximately 1.14.

Fisher's concept of the mean impact, later reinterpreted by Popper and other scholars, signifies a combination of two key factors: the selection of subsets based on attribute S, and the resulting increase in the frequency of attribute E within those subsets. We examine the relationship between Popper's interpretation of the mean impact and inference to the best explanation. We find that the mean impact does not adequately capture causal significance, as demonstrated by a counter-example, and develop criteria for identifying genuine cases of non-accidental increase in the mean impact. These criteria show that an entity or intervention causes an increase in the mean impact of a property E only when it itself causes property E. Consequently, the mean impact is not a suitable tool for identifying causal relationships.

Assisting human locomotion by providing external forces can help reduce the energy needed to move, but current systems requiring continuous propulsion face challenges with stability, control and efficiency. A new approach utilizes intermittent propulsion to support bipedal walking, maintaining assistive forces during specific phases and withdrawing them during others. This strategy uses a proactive control system that generates propulsion based on predictive models, rather than relying on external sensors or predefined trajectories. This ensures that the assistance provided aligns with the person's intended motion. We developed a predictor controller and validation mechanism to manage the uncertainties in monitoring a person's movement. Simulations with a well-studied human model demonstrated that this control strategy effectively synchronizes assistance with the model's dynamics. Experimental tests on a full-scale humanoid robot confirmed that the predictor control method is robust and generalizable.

This research proposes a visual relocalization technique based on 3D surfel maps.
The method utilizes learned features to match image patches with 3D surfels,
projecting the closest surfel according to depth predictions from a neural network.
A probabilistic framework then rejects outliers to compute an essential matrix,
resulting in accurate camera pose estimation even in challenging conditions such as
total illumination failure or extensive vegetation.
Compared to existing techniques, this approach demonstrates improved accuracy in both
2D position and orientation under various scenarios, with comprehensive testing in simulated and real environments.

The semi-supervised learning (SSL) approach leverages a substantial body of unlabeled data to enhance knowledge representation and classification accuracy by exploiting the principle that valid data samples should reside at the core of the feature space. Nonetheless, data distributions derived from unlabeled data often introduce biases that distort the model. To mitigate this issue, Federated SSL (FSSL) combines SSL with federated learning, permitting both labeled and unlabeled data to be utilized in a decentralized setting. To address these challenges, we introduce Ambiguity Reduction (AMBER), a novel technique designed to clarify the model's decision boundaries with regard to unlabeled data and mitigate the influence of data distribution biases. AMBER achieves this by identifying and removing the ambiguity inherent in unlabeled data, effectively reducing model ambiguity and enabling the model to better generalize to unknown data. The efficacy of AMBER is substantiated by experimental results, which show improvements in accuracy of up to 5.16%, 4.94%, and 4.3% for FashionMNIST, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100 datasets, respectively.

A novel algorithm has been developed for generating a sequence that converges consistently to a solution obtained through the Q-procedure, addressing both convex and non-convex optimization problems. The solution involves reformulating the optimization problem as a non-conviq fixed-point problem and applying the Osher-Schneider operator, whose fixed point corresponds to the solution of the optimization problem. The proposed algorithm applies the Shor method to this operator.

A system composed of a graphene sheet and closely spaced nanoparticles on one side and on the other side, separated by a thin spacer, exhibits specific plasmonic behavior.  When light hits the graphene sheet, resonance occurs at specific frequencies determined by the position of the nanoparticles and their associated plasmonic modes.  This resonance can be controlled by adjusting the electron density of the graphene.  Furthermore, when polarized terahertz light interacts with the graphene, it exhibits distinct resonances connected to both the in-plane and out-of-plane plasmonic modes of the electrons.

Patients who visit the emergency department due to minor injuries or
illnesses often experience a gradual decline in their symptom severity over time.
The duration of time spent treating such patients depends on when their symptoms
disappear, as determined by their response to therapy. In order to understand what
factors influence treatment outcomes, researchers examined patients' responses to
therapy among 853,233 individuals who received minimal care in a major emergency
department between 2009 and 2015. Their analysis revealed that such patients'
responses to therapy typically follow a consistent pattern, with approximately 50%
experiencing improvement, 25% experiencing no change, and another 25% experiencing
deterioration in their condition. Additionally, researchers discovered significant
differences in these patients' responses based on their presenting symptoms or
complaints, with近40% of patients who received antibiotics exhibiting improvement,
compared to近30% of other patients. Furthermore, researchers observed regional
variations in patients' responses, with some areas demonstrating higher levels of
improvement and others demonstrating higher levels of deterioration in their
condition. The researchers emphasized the importance of developing therapy models
for specific conditions, rather than generalizing therapy models for all patients.

This research proposes a cooperative approach for agents in tactical scenarios, operating within constrained network environments, even when disconnected, using only on-board resources. The method relies entirely on each agent's local capabilities, avoiding dependency on infrastructure. We tested this in challenging conditions resembling field deployments, with significant delays in communication and no infrastructure support, relying solely on simple network connections. Our findings, using standard planning and mapping tools typically not suitable for such environments, demonstrate that this method is feasible.

Our investigation of chiral magnetic effects in high-energy heavy-ion collisions has been carried out. We examined data collected during Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC, specifically at $\sqrt{\it{s}_{\mathrm{NN}}}$ = 2.76 and 5.02 TeV. To track possible signals of the influence of chiral magnetic effects on the movement of charged particles in these collisions, we linked groups of four charged particles and looked at two properties: their momentum in a plane and their spin in three dimensions. We created linked structures based on the electric charge of the particles and analyzed these properties with regard to the overall movement and shape of the particle collisions. Additionally, we looked at these properties relative to the direction the colliding particles moved in the horizontal plane. These associations were then compared to calculations made using a statistical model of particle interactions. We found no significant evidence that the properties were influenced by the process of breaking symmetry in these collisions or by the interaction between electric charge and magnetic fields. We have set limits on how much this influence could exist, and our findings are consistent with the observations reported in proton collisions at higher energies.

Over 6.5 million people rely on online fundraising, which has transformed into a crucial tool for connecting with potential supporters and tracking the dissemination of causes via crowd indicators. Despite the widespread use of online fundraising, there's limited research on the online activities of fundraisers. Consequently, the study's objective is to investigate the impact of crowd indicators on the effectiveness of online fundraising, independent of the platform. The analysis involves the examination of more than 1.5 million fundraising profiles, collected through an API-based approach. Findings suggest that the diversity of demographic factors such as gender, age, geographic distribution, and the frequency of activity can positively influence the amount raised. Conversely, the presence of personal information and the use of video content can negatively affect the amount raised. Notably, the impact of crowd indicators on fundraising success varies slightly across different platforms, although it's evident that online crowd indicators play a significant role in the effectiveness of fundraising efforts.

A rapidly growing number of cyber threats and their intricate relationships make it challenging for organizations to stay informed about emerging patterns, leading to an even harder time identifying emerging threats. To address this issue, a proposal for a federated learning-based exchange framework has been introduced. This framework allows organizations to collaborate on network breach detection and identify emerging patterns in breach data, all without sharing sensitive information. Several essential federated learning algorithms have been evaluated for this framework's development, and extensive simulations using real-world breach data have demonstrated its effectiveness and reliability.

Our research centers on optimizing the order of multi-point manipulation operations performed by a single robotic arm to enhance efficiency by reducing travel time, thereby improving the robot's performance in tasks involving multiple points. We've developed a novel approach that leverages unsupervised learning to order multi-point manipulation operations, and studied the impact of sequence on execution time, particularly in the context of pick-and-place tasks. Based on the identification of pivotal movement phases, we've established the significance of sequence, and addressed the issue through clustering techniques, starting with the assessment of two-point sequencing and subsequently extending this knowledge to order n points, revealing improvements in efficiency and pick placement accuracy. The findings demonstrate the effectiveness of our multi-point manipulation ordering strategy in increasing efficiency and dictating operation sequence, thereby proving its value even for tasks involving a small number of points, and highlighting the potential of this approach to yield substantial time savings for more complex tasks.

This study introduces silicon MOSFETs with high transfer transconductance and flexibility. The research focuses on enhancing transfer and channel properties by utilizing heavily doped source/drain regions and highly resistive channel areas. In addition, the SiMOSFETs were fabricated using standard 300mm CMOS technology. Results in 4H-silicon carbide showed high SiMOSFET performance in both positive and negative gate voltage directions, with n-type devices displaying a mobility of 160 cm2/Vs and p-type devices showing 108 cm2/Vs. These results highlight the feasibility of utilizing standard CMOS technology for the SiMOSFETs.

In adaptive systems, the concept of synchrony plays a significant role. In this study, two methods for assessing synchrony in adaptive systems are introduced, and their potential applications are explored. However, synchrony assessment poses significant challenges, primarily due to parameter variations within system subsets, which can hinder synchronization. To address this concern, a novel synchrony measure is developed, suitable for parameter mismatches. The proposed measures also enable evaluation of synchrony within groups and offer a metric for determining intergroup links. Illustrative examples, including coupled map lattices and adaptive systems based on the winning-stay, losing-split rule, are used to demonstrate the proposed synchrony measures.

User interfaces with high-quality search results are essential for video search. Unfortunately, current video search algorithms are flawed: they produce the top-ranked results frequently, but these are often subpar. To mitigate this issue, we are developing a benchmark using AI-based characters in videos that enables a more rigorous evaluation of how the diversity of sources affects search result quality. This framework will aid in quantifying variation bias among the top video search results. Moreover, our approach will enable a better understanding of the relationship between the rank of relevance and diversity. Ultimately, this innovation will empower video search algorithms to prioritize video content in a more accurate and reliable manner.

We begin our investigation into whether Monodromy Anomalies exist in a supersymmetric Wess-Zumino model. By utilizing the S-matrix framework, we derive an explicit formula for the model's scattering amplitudes with both helicity and chirality constraints. Building on this formula, we test the Monodromy Anomalies for various numbers of external particles. We find the anomalies hold in lower-order processes but encounter an inconsistency in the six-particle amplitude that suggests the anomalies do not fit within the supersymmetric framework. Additionally, we verify our findings for a specific tree-level process.

In current stochastic access systems, the medium-access probability is a fixed value predetermined during system setup, which does not take into account interference relationships between devices and channels. As a result, devices with unimpeded access to multiple channels may take precedence over those experiencing significant interference, leading to underutilization of affected devices and overloading of the remaining interference-free channels. Such a phenomenon causes a disparity in stochastic access performance, analogous to a hidden access privilege. Hence, we propose a variable stochastic access protocol that adjusts the medium-access probability based on interference relationship, with the objective of minimizing the objective function representing the disparity in successful transmission probabilities, or equivalently, achieving a uniform distribution of interference, or minimizing the required objective function to meet a given data rate requirement, or optimally assigning devices to channels to meet a given data rate requirement, or to maximize the objective function representing the system's overall efficiency.

Achieving accurate predictions in node, edge, and graph classification tasks using Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) with a scarcity of labels is a persistent challenge. Current approaches relying on pseudo-labeling employ simple classification targets, such as soft labels or median labels, generated using GNNs trained on a subset of accurately labeled data. However, these methods using single unified models often result in model overconfidence and performance degradation on previously unlabeled data. Graph relabeling methods using ensemble models show promise in generating high-quality pseudo-labels, but they struggle with data correction due to the generation of unreliable or inaccurate labels. 

This study introduces a novel pseudo-tagting graph learning approach that addresses these limitations by introducing two "tagting curves" to produce reliable multi-expert pseudo-labels and correct them on node, edge, and graph classification tasks. The first curve, the Tagting Ensemble Model (TEM), combines the labels from multi-expert models and refines them to eliminate noise. The second curve, the Tagting GNN (TGGN), integrates the refined labels with GNN to learn and adapt multi-expert models, ensuring they do not dominate each other. TGC offers consistent performance gains for GNN ensembles and multi-expert graphs with limited labels in node, edge, and graph classification tasks.

Video analysis on a massive scale has become increasingly important across various fields, including action recognition and video retrieval, where videos are often unstructured and numerous. Video features based on local templates require matching every frame across two videos, a computationally expensive process. We propose PatchNet, a lightweight and scalable network for local template correspondence, achieving improved efficiency without sacrificing accuracy. By focusing on the shortest distances between patches, we circumvent long-distance matches, reducing computational costs. Additionally, our proposed patch-level loss function leverages a self-organizing mechanism to group similar patches, extracting a small subset for training and thus lowering overall computational expenses. We also introduce a rapid, efficient distance metric for evaluating patch similarity, replacing the commonly used cosine metric and yielding tangible time savings. Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in two prominent benchmarks, revealing substantial efficiency gains with comparable accuracy. Notably, we observe a 7.5x-80x speedup in computing template costs and a 7.5x improvement in inference time for video feature extraction.

We modify the one-dimensional discrete-time asymmetric exclusion process by introducing $k-1$ additional site exclusion rules, resulting in a model where a single occupancy site is allowed for groups of up to $k$ consecutive particles. Our analysis of the modified model reveals how its one-step master equation can be transformed into a higher-dimensional equation with $k$ dimensions, using a mapping that relates its dynamics to a generalized asymmetric exclusion process with specific boundary conditions. Additionally, we apply this mapping to calculate how changes in the model affect particle current with respect to initial conditions for a specific class of starting configurations. A specific case of this modified model is explored in more detail through examples of particle current calculations and a connection to the exclusion process with site-specific reflection rules.

A novel wireless power transfer method known as simultaneous wireless information and power transfer (SWIPT) has the potential to revolutionize the development of green wireless systems. This paper investigates a SWIPT-enabled orthogonal frequency-division multiple access (OFDMA) network by examining the efficient allocation of power and subchannels. Under the SWIPT framework, base stations receive energy from a central source, and the computed power distribution maximizes the overall system data rate while complying with various constraints. This problem is decomposed into manageable sub-problems, and an iterative algorithm is developed to solve them. The simulation results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm successfully achieves a substantial improvement in system data rate with optimal power distribution and meets the requirements for simultaneous energy and information transfer.

This study explores the impact of low-density limits on SU(N) Fermi mixtures with repulsive interactions, focusing on hyperrepulsive, just-attractive, and with an additional phase, the 'N-ary' phase. Utilizing the Fermi-Dirac distribution and expanding just-attractive parameters with respect to low-density and velocity, just-attractive parameters were found. An interesting observation was that, in low-density limits, just-attractive parameters were found to be independent of the number of colors N, suggesting a pattern of color universality. A theoretical analysis using the diagrammatic expansion was conducted, which indicated that, in low-density limits, just-attractive parameters were determined by the same leading-order term. Just-attractive parameters were found for SU(2) with repulsive delta interactions and additional hyperrepulsive interactions, which contrasted with a previously observed color-universal behavior in the same systems. An attempt was made to understand this apparent contradiction. It was discovered that, in low-density limits, the just-attractive parameter for repulsive delta interactions followed a pattern of $N$-dependence ($\propto N$), which was consistent with the previously observed color-universal behavior. However, this pattern of $N$-dependence was found to be independent of the low-density and velocity. We present a simple electrical circuit model of superconducting DR-mechanical oscillators that accurately reflects the impact of the radiative reaction force. Our findings indicate that the circuit's equivalent inductance can be interpreted as the mechanical oscillator's mass, the equivalent capacitance as its compliance, and the resistive component as the damping force. Furthermore, we demonstrate that energy dissipation in the mechanical system results from ohmic heating in the coupled electrical circuit.

The definition of Airy polynomials arises from a modified form of the classical Airy integrals, resulting in modified Airy functions and modified Bessel functions of the first kind. At its core, the work presents a modified change of variables in order to maintain invariance under modifications to the integrand. Additionally, the study obtains modified Airer functions and modified Geiser equations as a direct consequence.

Mobile robots encountering sudden changes in environment, such as unexpected boundaries, can become trapped. We investigate the dynamics of a robot navigating a change in environment from open to confined, using a setup where an adhering robot moves along a straight path and suddenly encounters a vertical barrier. Starting from various initial positions, the robot's movement is influenced by a combination of forces, including a direction-changing potential and sticky elasticity, causing it to either adhere to the barrier or remain in the open space. An boundary parameter determines the behavior, causing the robot to switch between adhering to the barrier and not adhering to it in the limit. This transition is identified as an instance of historical unpredictability, where the robot's movement on either side of the boundary is qualitatively different, yet the boundary itself is quickly crossed and the results on both sides become indistinguishable. This type of limit cycle bifurcation, in addition to being unstable, underlies the phenomenon of unpredictability in situations like this.

This article explores the development of 2-dimensional fermionic scalar field theory within the pAQFT framework, focusing on achieving a covariant time evolution in global Minkowski spacetime. The analysis delves into key aspects such as the role of a chirality operator in the free theory, the handling of the caustic in interacting scenarios, and a detailed examination of the caustic in specific Minkowski spacetime subsets.

Two common methods for automatically detecting smoke in laparoscopic videos are template matching and deep learning, each has strengths and weaknesses. While template matching often lacks sufficient performance on its own, deep learning models often struggle with limited availability of annotated smoke data. A research team investigated whether enhancing smoke image quality through image improvement techniques could boost the effectiveness of template matching. They compared the effectiveness of two image improvement methods - contrast enhancement and color deconvolution - on the performance of a pre-trained deep learning model used for template matching. Results revealed that color deconvolution consistently improved template matching performance across multiple runs, surpassing the performance of template matching without image improvement and comparing favorably to a recently published deep learning model for smoke detection.

To minimize errors in multi-qubit Molmer-Sorensen gates using trapped ions, we need to achieve motion-damping. This can be challenging when multi-frequency laser noise couples with the ions' modes, creating a complex frequency pattern known as anti-correlation, which we need to control. We recommend using an approach where the laser frequencies are applied in pairs to the ions, ensuring that the noise effects are consistent across all modes. This allows for motion elimination through a process called spin-mixing, streamlining the MS gate operation even in noisy environments.

The mechanism behind the dielectric, nonferroelectric state of titanates, particularly in relation to how it transitions into a ferroelectric state and a antiferroelectric phase is linked to similar structural distortions, has been challenging to explain through theoretical models. However, by applying machine learning algorithms, we successfully derived atomic-scale models for several key dielectric titanates directly from experimentally measured neutron scattering data. These models, characterized as having no net dipole and no specific preferred structure, exhibit a dynamic structure where the titanium atoms are in a fourfold coordinated state. We further validated our results by demonstrating that even a minor introduction of a B-site cation valence anomaly within these atomic-scale models is sufficient to trigger a phase transition to a ferroelectric or antiferroelectric phase. Additionally, our results indicate that the characteristics of these atomic-scale models are also responsible for the occurrence of a soft transverse optical mode observed in experiments.

Multivariate data analysis often encounters challenges related to high dimensionality and correlation structure complexity. Graphical Gaussian processes offer a solution by linking multivariate processes with graphs, thereby imposing constraints on the mean, covariance, and regularization patterns. This integration enables precise modeling of patterns across multiple dimensions and simplifies inference using standard tools. In contrast, Functional Gaussian graphical models separately model and regularize the function and correlation components, leading to distinct but similar methods. This paper establishes a connection between these approaches, showing that some functional Gaussian graphical models can be represented as graphical processes, leading to efficient alternative inference methods and clear insights into estimation consistency, particularly in the context of estimation via conditional likelihood.

Standard quantum circuit compilation methods often rely on dynamic vertex coloring of a graph, but this approach can result in an excessively long quantum circuit. Several graph coloring methods exist, yet for large and repeatedly patterned quantum circuits, these are typically outperformed by our novel algorithm. Our algorithm efficiently constructs a long-and-repeated graph and determines a vertex coloring in time proportional to the number of repeated patterns, ultimately producing a shorter quantum circuit.

The primary objective of this research is to establish average-case tail estimates for the number of iterations $T$ needed in a convex optimization algorithm such that the probability of exceeding the threshold $t$ diminishes exponentially, denoted as ${\mathbb P}(T > t) \le e^{-ct}$. However, the probability of exceeding five times the threshold decreases only fractionally, represented by ${\mathbb P}(T > 5t) \le ve^{-ct}$. The proof relies on a novel approach, the "tail-only" approach, which is based on the fact that the algorithm converges faster than median or mean times, resulting in significantly fewer converging algorithm runs beyond these points, thus allowing the derivation of tight tail bounds from convergence characteristics. Additionally, the $\frac vd+$ five condition is shown to be unnecessary, resulting in an open question regarding the validity of the $T > 3t$ case. The validation of these estimates is demonstrated through experiments involving power method analysis of high-dimensional random matrices.

This study proposes an innovative, robust method for radio-based localization and tracking that leverages communication links and is resilient to interference from dedicated localization signals. The suggested approach integrates local adaptation with communication transfer, allowing it to utilize known communication antennas to reduce the number of required dedicated antennas. The inherent advantages of using dedicated antennas, such as simplified design and lower costs, remain accessible, while the need for communication antennas can be further reduced. The proposed method combines a interference-rejecting adaptive filter and common signal processing techniques shared between communication and localization domains to facilitate data transfer. Simulation results demonstrate the superiority of this adaptive approach over traditional methods that rely on dedicated signals and interference rejection.

The systematic study combines theoretical and experimental investigations to explore the complex polarisation states of multiple gauge bosons, a crucial aspect for testing the Standard Model and searching for new phenomena beyond current models. This research combines field theory calculations, Monte Carlo simulations, and experimental data to analyze the polarisation states of $W^{\pm}Z$ bosons produced in $p$ $p$ collisions. Utilizing the reconstruction of helicity and polar angle states, this study employs ATLAS detector results at a 13 TeV center-of-mass energy to constrain the long-range forces involved in the process through likelihood analysis, comparing total and differential cross-sections to measurements.

Oda and Watanabe previously demonstrated that ortholattices of subsets of a set and relations on that set are dual to each other, according to a specificlattice characterization. Building upon this foundation, we generalize this concept to orthocomplemented lattices with subsets, providing a theorempresenting pairs of structures in terms of relations, and illustrating itsapplication with a primary example: ortholattices of subspaces within vector spacesover a field.

We introduce a proof script visualizer built upon a proof assistant's proof search engine. This proof visualizer enables users to observe proof scripts generated by the proof explorer in coq-psv, thereby identifying more efficient tactics to complete given goals. Additionally, it allows proof assistant developers to analyze and design new proof search engine strategies by identifying scripts produced by the proof explorer and those generated by the engine itself. Our tool was developed using coq, git, and coq-proof-script-analysis, which is a program for extracting proof scripts from coq.

We derive an exact upper limit on the maximum L4 norm of Hecke cusp forms within specific subspaces of cusp forms, defined by minimal weight and level constraints. This is achieved by refining an initial estimate proposed by Soundararajan, leveraging improvements from the level aspect, and carefully selecting the relevant subspace of cusp forms. As a result, we confirm the validity of Soundararajan's conjecture for such subspaces, and we also obtain precise L4 norm estimates for Hecke cusp forms in the forms newforms and certain other newforms under the level aspect, thus resolving a problem initially posed by the authors in an earlier study.

Interior Point Methods (IPMs), a subset of Elliptic Optimization Methods, are employed to address Charnes-Cooper and quadratic reformulations of Convex Optimization Problems (COPs), including Non-Linear Programming, Semidefinite Optimization, and Semidefinite Conic Optimization, as detailed in [1, 2].

Interior Point Methods utilize Krylov solvers to tackle Linear Programming and Conic Programming components within each iteration. However, the accuracy of these solutions directly impacts IPM progress, necessitating reliable termination criteria for Krylov solvers, which often prove elusive.

This research investigates Non-Linear Programming reformulations, examining relative residual and absolute residual termination criteria through numerical experiments, utilizing MUMPS as the Linear Programming solver and OSCAR2 as the Solving Operator Counter. The findings indicate that relative residual can result in premature termination, whereas absolute residual ensures sufficient precision to drive IPM progress, even if the Final Status of the Krylov solver indicates failure.

A transition matrix element is the key to the variable flavor count approach, and we have computed its leading twist, spin-dependent, and strange-quark flavor-singlet component to the next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) in the context of QCD with four flavors. Calculated at $x x x$, the results are expressed in terms of $\alpha_s$ and are valid for $\sigma\sigma$ values of 3, 4, and 5. By applying a novel algorithm, we solved the relevant differential equations and utilized the nnnlo formula to facilitate this computation. Furthermore, our findings are benchmarked against the next-to-next-to-leading order (nnlo) calculations for the spin-independent, strange-quark contribution, as well as the next-to-next-to-leading order (nnlo) and spin-dependent next-to-next to leading order (nnlo) of the valence and axial-vector distributions, respectively, under the five-flavor, or $\sigma\sigma$ = 5, framework.

When developed correctly, AI has the potential to significantly reshape our lives for the better, but historical precedents suggest that erroneous AI has also caused substantial harm. Current AI incidents reported online are shrouded in inaccuracies, hindering researchers from gaining a clear understanding of the AI incident landscape. To address this issue, we introduce the AI Incident Repository (AIR), the first comprehensive catalog of real-world AI incidents. Consisting of 861 incidents from 49 distinct categories, the repository provides context and specific performance metrics for each entry, enabling researchers to analyze patterns, such as the repercussions of using unreliable AI-driven systems. The repository is available at https://ai-incidents.org for free use.

We've developed an accurate method for solving the Renormalization Group equations by simulating the gradient descent process of these equations in functional space. Our approach Renormalization Group Fixed Point Search algorithm enables the precise renormalization of these equations and resulting theory, achieving exceptional agreement with analytical standards on simple models of the Renormalization Group, specifically a scalar field theory in four-dimensional space and the Wilson-Fisher theory in three dimensions.

Human interaction design often relies on dual-process specifications that ensure safety and liveness requirements are met during human system interactions. Despite their importance, effectively verifying these specifications in complex systems can be challenging, especially if the designer and development team lack expertise in formal methods. In this research, we introduce a framework called dispute management to tackle this issue. An operator uses the framework to pinpoint and highlight issues within a dual-process specification during a human system interaction. Following the operator's input, the framework revises the original specification to accommodate any discoveries made. Furthermore, we formalize this framework using automata theory to guarantee that the revised specification adheres to the original requirements and meets all safety and liveness requirements. Additionally, we showcase a successful application of this framework in a dual-process specification relevant to cardiac surgery.

We define the theoretical framework for an imperative hardware description language called Proto-Quipper-M, which is a subset of the Quantum Ising Machine Language, through an approach that maps the language to a weaker version of the lambda-calculation simultaneously evaluation semantics used for theoretical Java. This theoretical framework serves as the foundation for understanding the language's intended behavior. We examine the language's design choices in relation to its stronger counterpart, expressing these decisions within an iterative fixed-point approach simultaneous evaluation lambda-calculation. We demonstrate how our theoretical framework accurately represents the intended meaning of Proto-Quipper-M by proving that it is a conservative extension of Proto-Quipper.

We utilize the resolvent equation to derive an expression for the density of eigenvalue distributions of a broad class of random matrices, and we demonstrate that this expression can determine the large-n asymptotic behavior of these distributions, allowing us to locate and analyze critical points of the spectra. The method established provides a convenient framework for investigating the limiting density of eigenvalues, facilitating examination of critical points and edge characteristics of the spectra. The method's applicability to and validation with several well-known random matrix models demonstrate its utility, and the framework can be used to determine and analyze the outlier behavior of certain non-given random matrix models. The method's capacity to locate and investigate spectral thresholds and edges allows for the analysis of the fluctuation behavior of outliers within these models.

A method is proposed for producing optical phases with minimal uncertainty in light 
by using an ensemble of atoms within an optical cavity and exploiting the interaction 
between the atoms' fermionic states and the cavity's electromagnetic field in the regime of strong coupling. 
The approach involves creating pairs of bosonic excitations through the flip of atomic states 
from dark states to a bright state, resulting in bosonic squeezing of the optical field and the possibility of achieving phase assessment with the Heisenberg limit of uncertainty. 
To minimize the impact of optical noise and reach the Heisenberg limit, 
it is essential to have extremely high reflection coefficients of the cavity, high fermionic coupling rates, 
large ensemble sizes, and precise pumping control. 
The outline of the experiment is also detailed, it entails an optical microcavity with highly reflective mirrors and a cold cloud of Rb-87 atoms with narrow (D1) and wide (D2) resonance lines. 
The D1 line is used for coupling through the application of microwave pulses, 
while the D2 transition is used for coupling with light and producing phase assessment.

As a crucial step in capturing the complete genome sequence of an organism, de novo short-read read assembly has seen a significant advancement with the introduction of long read sequencing technology. However, each new approach to long read sequencing technology presents its own challenges in addressing the extreme storage and computational requirements during genome assembly. We leverage the graph-based assembly concept to efficiently manage memory and processing power by creating a contiguous genome assembly in a distributed environment using a parallel creation algorithm. This innovative approach facilitates efficient genomes assembly in the face of massive datasets. We implemented this novel strategy within the framework of FRiCAS, a distributed memory parallel creation genome assembly software, which has been thoroughly evaluated on various datasets from different organisms.

A modified logistic equation, incorporating a time delay, models the growth of a population and is represented as y'(t) = ay(t)[1-y(t-D)/a], where D represents the delay in units of time. When the delay D exceeds zero, our study demonstrates that solutions remain bounded, globally exist, and maintain positivity for all y(t) when 1-D is greater than zero. However, if the delay surpasses 1, certain scenarios may lead to the solution becoming unbounded or non-existent, a phenomenon attributed to oscillatory dynamics within the system.

The traditional regression depth extends the concept of multivariate depth to point processes, using the Euclidean distance between predicted and actual values, measured as the number of points. However, this interpretation relies on the assumption that the response variable adheres to a Gaussian distribution, which limits its applicability to non-Gaussian processes. To address this shortcoming, we propose a statistical depth extension that overcomes this restriction by transforming point patterns into the plane and utilizing the Fréchet distance to evaluate the discrepancy between observed and expected predictions. The proposed method employs the Isometric Log-Change transformation to convert the Euclidean Fréchet distance into a computationally efficient form.

We investigate the capabilities of an advanced superconducting electrical hybrid device, composed of two Mesoscopic Superconducting Entities (MSEs), and propose a cutting-edge method to achieve perfect energy transfer. Each MSE, and thus the entire system, consists of two Josephson circuits. One subset of Josephson junctions is connected to a coherent photon source, while the other is coupled with two DC-SQUIDs. By fine-tuning the parameters of the MSEs, we demonstrate enhanced quantum characteristics and significant amplification of the Josephson phase oscillations. Subsequently, we apply a periodic magnetic flux pulse and adjust the frequencies of the coherent photon source and magnetic flux pulse in unison. This synchronized approach yields the perfect transfer of oscillated energy within the system.

Atomic properties were examined in a study involving three germanium isotopes - $^{62}$Ge, $^{64}$Ge, and $^{65}$Ge - each with an unpaired proton in the $d$-shell. The isotopes were analyzed using high-precision isotope-specific laser spectroscopy, yielding precise atomic moments. The study found that the isotopic shift in the $^{62}$Ge to $^{64}$Ge range aligns with predictions from a modified harmonic oscillator model, confirming that two neutron shells are filled up to $N$ = 40. The $d$-shell magnetic moment for the unpaired proton in $^{62}$Ge and $^{64}$Ge matched calculations based on the shell model. Additionally, the study found a $l$ = $3/2$ contribution in $^{65}$Ge, indicating $d$-$p$ configuration mixing. The study also measured the $p$-component of the magnetic moment for an $N$ = 40, $J^{\pi} = 2^+$ state at 1709 keV in $^{62}$Ge, marking a first time this component was directly measured.

The development of a cutting-edge isochronous mass spectrometry technique relies on the precise determination of the $a_{IP}$ factor, which is the product of the IP mass and the $\beta$-factor. This development is crucial for achieving high-accuracy measurements of the masses of short-lived, exotic nuclei. A cutting-edge method for determining the $a_{IP}$ factor individually for each ion utilizes digital tracking and precise steering based on the nucleus's magnetic rigidity. This approach minimizes the impact of uncertainties associated with the ion source and beam dynamics. As a result, the $a_{IP}$ factor for each ion can be experimentally determined. This approach was applied at the CSR at RI Beam Factory for measuring the $^{229}$Th mass. It enabled the reduction of the relative measurement uncertainty to 2.1E-10, thereby providing the most accurate, to date, determination of this mass and enabling the precise testing of theoretical predictions for nuclear binding energies and the nuclear ground-state spin-parity.

explained in depth, accompanied by illustrations of its application to a simple
spin system and a lattice field theory. Finally, the document concludes with
