Identifying unlabelled structured text such as emails, using a non-convex optimisation method that incorporates the results of an NLP model and the effectiveness of text extraction through regular expressions, achieves high accuracy without the need for a segmentation model, significantly reducing the number of false positives compared to existing methods. Testing on the TREC collection of texts, this approach outperforms the top-rated method, particularly in detecting less common structured texts like contact information and phone numbers, while also exploring the effects of different segmentation methods on regular expression performance.

Our research focuses on the distinct characteristics of the proton-nucleus cross-section that can help identify the existence of the top quark. A model, derived from the finite size and structural properties of the proton and nucleus, has been used to calculate the cross-section. Comparisons between the proton-nucleus and electron-nucleon cross-section ratios, particularly at high energies where the quark fractional charges can be related to the top quark, are presented. The proton-nucleus total cross-section data is also examined to search for an abnormal increase that could be attributed to top quark production. The study's findings support the presence of an anomalous increase in the total proton-proton cross-section at the proton accelerator accelerator facility HERA.

This research investigates cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, and proposes a novel framework that utilizes an integrated network to accomplish the task. The proposed framework, along with an auxiliary task, aims to enhance the cross-domain parsing capability and is evaluated on the benchmark dataset of the Spider dataset. Specific improvements on the framework include an adaptive integration module, modular and context-sensitive parsing head, and an additional auxiliary task for cross-domain learning. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that this new framework achieves superior performance on the cross-domain parsing task when compared to other current and traditional parsing methods.

A recent deep radio survey, the LOFAR Two-metre Sky Survey (initial data release), covered 900 square degrees of the Northern sky with great detail. This survey covered a wide frequency range from 136 to 168 MHz, corresponding to the 1.4 GHz band, and resolved sources as small as 2.5 arcseconds. Analyzing the brightness distribution of the survey, we found a clear power law relationship between source brightness and frequency for objects brighter than 0.35 mJy. This indicates the presence of highly energetic galaxies within the observed area. The data further revealed a overall galaxy bias pattern with respect to the galaxy mass, where more massive galaxies were found. However, we observed altered bias patterns at very low and very high galaxy masses. The study also found distinct relationships between the galaxy number and the galaxy mass, which varied depending on the mass range. Additionally, we found that approximately 10% of the energetic sources in the survey were not consistent with previous cataloged radio galaxies. These unusual sources may include lower-mass galaxies or galaxies with unusual properties.

The High-Dimensional Rank Lasso model effectively analyzes complex datasets with significant outliers, although solving it computationally is challenging. A revised OLS approach has been developed to address this issue, incorporating an adaptive-sifting technique and leveraging the EXPOL and EXCELLEX outliers metrics. Following the initial optimization of the EXPOL objective function using EXEX or EXCELLEX, the resulting matrix was inserted into the High-Dimensional Rank Lasso objective function and solved via the EXEX or EXCELLEX algorithms. This method efficiently tackles the High-Dimensional Rank Lasso problem, exceeding the performance of the Cox-Lasso and EXOLasso algorithms.

As key to understanding how energy is dissipated in quantum systems evolving over time, the concept of entropy generation has been applied to various contexts, including open and closed systems. However, its calculation often poses difficulties, especially when dealing with closed systems. Utilizing convex roof extensions, new formulas for entropy generation in pure-state dynamics have been developed and and and demonstrated for examples and for cases involving slow and mild driving conditions. Furthermore, it was found that the newly formulated bounds are reasonably close to previously established limits, thus offering a new perspective on entropy generation even when it cannot be directly computed.

Our research explores the ecological implications of AI technologies through the lens of technical systems theory. By examining how AI solutions interact with ecosystems, we uncover that the environmental impacts of AI technologies have been largely overlooked in current environmental accounting methods. In response, we develop a novel framework for assessing the environmental effects of AI in the case study of AI-powered environmental monitoring, revealing hidden ecological disruptions caused by the deployment of AI solutions. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the environmental disruptions caused by AI technologies will become even more significant as AI technologies become more deeply integrated into various sectors of the economy, necessitating a broader assessment of their ecological implications upon the global ecosystem.

Research into prescriptive procedure monitoring has been conducted for quite some time, yet the field's current state is not clear. We aim to resolve this ambiguity by creating a classification system that categorizes prescriptive procedure monitoring research based on their key characteristics. The framework, which considers the underlying research question, real-world setting, process being monitored, analysis techniques, and metrics used, allows for structured comparisons across studies. Upon reviewing 39 relevant papers from the last three decades, we found that existing monitoring research often struggles to accurately predict actual performance due to limited real-world testing and a lack of comprehensive results. Furthermore, there appears to be little progression in terms of methods used, potentially hindering a clear understanding of prescriptive procedure monitoring's capabilities. The proposed framework can help guide future research and highlight key areas for improvement.

This study delves into the posterior mistake control of the generalized heat transfer model for a substance, with a focus on its application to a material like silicon. The investigation begins by breaking down the heat transfer problem into its constituent parts, including its non-linear nature and the interconnection between temperature and density through the Akenine-Chapman-Marsh model. The study then identifies various sources of error and measures their impact on the achievement of multiple, distinct objectives, utilizing a measure of sensitivity for each objective. By employing local approximations, the investigation develops an expression for error measurement and identifies specific areas where mistakes can be reduced effectively. Furthermore, the study introduces a novel approach to material heating optimization, combining the minimization of a specific objective function with a limited amount of energy. This optimization process is carried out in an inverse problem setting, and the study demonstrates its effectiveness through two exemplary simulations, showcasing significant improvements in sensitivity reduction and overall objective function performance.

Machine learning's stacking ensemble method boasts strong predictive capabilities.
The idea is to combine diverse models in two steps. First, a first set of models,
called level 1 models, predict outcomes for given data points. Then, a second set, level 2, uses these predictions as inputs to make a final prediction.
We've discovered that for specific scenarios with two classes, the analysis can be simplified.
We define maximum limits on the number of data points and attributes that need to be considered, and provide an program that applies these simplified constraints.
We've also provided similar results for scenarios involving more than two classes.
We've also explored the scenarios where one model at level 2 makes a difference,
showing that in these cases, the program can be designed to solve the issue directly,
similar to solving a puzzle, by using models and analyzing data points.

The structure of the game is not known to the players, so they form beliefs about how the game is set up and what moves the other players will make. The strategy "ensure" means a player chooses a move that maximizes the payoff no matter what the structure of the game is. However, if there are many moves to choose from, "ensure" might not even give the player the best possible outcome in every scenario. We look at repeated interactions between players who have strong initial beliefs about the structure of the game. The game structure is initially agreed upon by most players, so small groups of players might have different beliefs. In our model, a preferential interaction occurs when the structure of the game is changed in a way that reflects these beliefs. The player who benefits from their initial understanding of the structure is more likely to influence the decision on how the structure is changed. Over time, the interaction leads to a convergence of beliefs among the majority of players. The concept of "limited assurance" explains this focused interaction where most players agree on the structure, but there are incentives for some to try and change it. We show that the long-term interaction will lead to the majority of players agreeing on the structure that can be ensured by "ensure" in the limited assurance sense. This concept also explains how the players' initial understanding of the structure will persist over the long term.

Recent developments in holographic duality suggest that asymptotic level fuzziness at a boundary can be represented by black holes with negligible fluctuations and temperature approaching zero. Researchers have determined the geometric interior of these black holes by analyzing the internal connections of their complex, temperature-independent properties. Building on this foundation, this research explores a scenario where the geometric interior of these black holes represents the quantum mechanics of a matter system in a nearly pure state. Within this framework, the geometric time parameter corresponds to the system's complex evolution. Additionally, this study explores how entangling degrees of freedom within the system can create geometric structures, such as bridges, and how this entanglement affects the time parameter. Furthermore, it examines how pure states can access the deep geometric interior of these black holes, thus defining their internal structure through matter properties.

To accurately model the behavior of living systems, we must understand their underlying atomic processes, such as how individual molecules and their aggregates form and interact to create emergent properties. RNA production dynamics are crucial for understanding transcription dynamics, yet their overall pattern across an entire cell remains unclear. To address this question, we conducted a comprehensive simulation of RNA production across the entire cell of yeast across several conditions. By comparing our results to global measurements of RNA abundance, we found that different yeast genes do not always reach a steady state at the same time, and that post-transcriptional regulation can affect the overall timing of RNA production, in addition to its typical influence on RNA stability.

The concurrent occurrence of rotational modes in the ground and excited 0+ states of 64Ni is investigated. By applying the monopole tensor interaction within the antisymmetrized molecular orbital no-core shell model, we are able to replicate the experimentally observed rotational energies at null spin. This approach yields a more accurate description of the 64Ni nucleus, compared to the results obtained using the mean-field and single-particle models.

Chiral SU(Nc) SQCD with Nf (where f is less than or equal to 11) flavors exhibits an anomaly which results in a gauge symmetry breaking. To prevent this, we explore three sets of spin-1/2 Wess-Zumino supermultiplet contents that can match the chiral SU(Nc) theory's indices for anomaly indices. These sets consist of Nf pairs of (Q, bar Q) quark supermultiplets, Nf triplets of (D, bar D), (Phi, bar Phi) hypermultiplets, and a singlet supermultiplet S, and we investigate whether these sets can (i) generate a non-perturbative Witten anomaly and lead to supersymmetry breaking; (ii) produce a non-perturbative gauge symmetry that results in supersymmetry breaking. Our analysis reveals that these sets fail to meet these criteria except in one instance: (i) results in an SU(Nf) duality; (ii) leads to a Sp(Nf) duality; (iii) yields an SO(Nf+2) duality.

A linear complementary set of group codes over a finite principal ideal domain (PID) $D$ with a finite residue field $D/M$ ($M$ a maximal ideal of $D$) means a collection of subcodes with the full rank of $D^n$ when summed together. We establish a criterion for determining whether the direct sum of three group codes over a specific type of PID ($M^2$ in characteristic 2 or $p^2$ otherwise) is full rank. This criterion leads to the development of algorithms that efficiently find a linear complementary set of group codes over the rings $D_2 = D \times D$ and $D_p = D/M^2$ with a finite field $D_p$ and prime $p$. We demonstrate the applicability of these algorithms on the integer integers $\mathbb{Z}$ and the Gaussian integers $\mathbb{G}$.

Recently, there has been a growing interest in using graphical models to represent complex functions, particularly in the fields of machine learning and optimization. This interest is driven by the need to tackle the limitations of graphical models, which are constrained by their structure, limiting their applicability in real-world problems. Overcoming these constraints would significantly expand the use of graphical models in high-demand applications, such as multi-agent reinforcement learning. However, the complexity of general graphical models has hindered their practical utilization. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel function depiction method that leverages graphical models to represent arbitrary functions, both in their continuous and discrete forms. This approach allows us to obtain precise maximum probability estimates and facilitates optimization through gradient-based methods, all while being agnostic to the specific nature of the functions being represented. We also explore the effects of the structure and the granularities of our framework, offering insights into the efficient representation of functions.

We introduce Asynchronous Audio Visual Fusion (AAVF), a straightforward yet powerful technique for identifying audio frames that incorporate audio signals from varying time points. AWFV is especially beneficial for the task of detecting items in video, as audio cues associated with specific objects may not be contained within the same frame. Our experiments demonstrate that AAVF significantly enhances object detection performance, when combined with basic fusion strategies. Notably, we observe performance improvements even in situations where audio signals prove irrelevant. AAVF can be evaluated using metrics such as the mean intersection over union and can be applied to object detection, tracking, and video classification.

A universal pattern of velocity field behavior has been discovered across different types of shear flow experiments in emulsions that undergo a sudden change in behavior. By analyzing measurements of flow speed at various distances from the boundary, we found that the emulsions' self-organization process is consistent across samples, regardless of their overall behavior. This is evidenced by a set of curves that converge when the distance from the boundary is scaled by each sample's characteristic distance from the boundary to the boundary. These unified patterns allow for comparison of the spatial structure of the flow within each sample at the respective characteristic distances, where a linear relationship between the distance from the boundary and the flow speed is observed, supported by previous research and theory.

This study presents electric load models for different periods of the power outage, 
leaving room for further analysis of the hourly electricity consumption pattern. 
To achieve this, we applied the method of moment matching to remain within the classification 
of linear systems for convenience. We start by collecting and preprocessing the data in 
an appropriate format, and then we determine the probability density function (PDF) of the 
random variable representing electricity consumption using a continuous approximation. 
Next, we carry out the matching of selected moments and construct the model, before 
validating it against the original data in an unsupervised setting. Finally, we utilize 
the model to determine the probability of specific events related to electricity usage.

To investigate the root cause of the homogeneity problem, we examined a controlled laboratory setting in which we measured individual observers' information acquisition during Google Web search. Our findings revealed that the customization of Web search results leads users to overlook relevant, perturbed information, and this effect explains the limited information acquisition in the public sphere as well. Our study demonstrates that the amount of pertinent information that may be missed due to search customization can account for up to 50% of total information available, and it highlights the necessity of accounting for observers' perceptions in models of information propagation.

Visual Communication Convolutional Neural Networks (VCO-CNN) are emerging as a promising solution for addressing the context loss issue in traditional CNNs when processing two-dimensional images. Although effective in recovering image context, VCO-CNNs come with increased computational costs. Our proposed Graph Recognition Convolutional Neural Networks (GRCNN) architecture leverages graph-based neurons to efficiently capture the structural characteristics of flow diagrams, enabling improved generalization. By utilizing the flexibility of graph-based neurons, GRCNN incorporates graph optimization costs as a form of regularization. Our experiments demonstrate the performance of GRCNN in generating correct programs from flow diagrams, which is more efficient compared to conventional context-aware CNNs.

This study offers a comprehensive summary of the mathematical foundation of climate models built upon partial differential equations (PDEs) and the numerical techniques of model simplification known as model contraction. Model contraction techniques, such as domain reduction, operator truncation, and time discretization, are explored with their respective consequences. It is demonstrated how these models retain essential features of the original physical systems they were derived from. While maintaining fidelity to the original models, successive contraction methods simplify computational demands, rendering high-resolution climate simulations feasible on limited hardware. The paper concludes by highlighting future research avenues in the field of contracted climate models.

The radiative behavior of a specific type of atom, mesne os, formed through a process called neutron capture, is analyzed using both theoretical modeling and experimental data.  This atom, os, and its similar variants, are found in the remnants of powerful celestial events known as kilonovae, which occur when certain types of stars collide.  The presence of elements like os in these remnant explosions allows us to learn more about how these reactions take place, particularly in terms of opacity, which affects the light emitted from these remnant explosions.  To learn more, we're simulating the properties of os and its similar variants by calculating the movements of its charged particles and comparing our results to experimental data.  This can then be applied to understand the creation of specific elements, including os, during kilonovae explosions, particularly in terms of how the charge of these variants affects their chemical behavior.  To accomplish this, we use a process called configuration interaction, involving data from high-energy remnant explosions, where the density and speed affect the movement of charged particles and their behavior.

The stomach, small and large intestines, are automatically identified and outlined within abdominal CT scans, using an unoptimized, deep learning-based approach. For this task, a dataset of CT scans and corresponding manual segmentations from the public NIH challenge is utilized. A U-Net model, trained on this data, achieves a Dice coefficient average of 0.74 for the organs in question. To address issues with ambiguous boundaries between these organs and other abdominal organs, two complementary algorithms are applied, increasing the Dice coefficient to 0.82. The final results demonstrate that the proposed approach allows for accurate and automated organ detection and segmentation.

Compositional data represents quantities that total a predefined amount and are often displayed as percentages. Traditionally, researchers have avoided using standard linear methods to analyze compositional data due to concerns that they would mask the interdependence of the components. Instead, a non-standard analytical approach was employed. Here, we address this issue by utilizing percentage values and ratio values to transform compositional data into a format suitable for linear analysis, ultimately interpreting the results within the framework of the simplex framework.

We analyzed radial velocity data from the CORALIE and HARPS instruments for 36 planets with masses under 10 Earth masses and orbital periods less than two years, orbiting around small and relatively cool stars. We found that none of these planets fit within the desert area between 0.85 to 13 Earth masses and the specified orbital periods, leading us to consider that the detection methods have significant biases. We found that stars with larger radii are more likely to be found with larger planets, which aligns with predictions from atmospheric scattering models. Our findings suggest that follow-up studies with space telescopes like TESS and JWST, along with simulations, are needed to better understand how these planets form.

Effective management of self-knowledge through attention is essential to prevent game-playing, thus enhancing the robustness of reinforcement learning agents. Present attention mechanisms in RL, like the VAE attention model (VAEAM), look ahead ahead to anticipate the target's movement, allowing the agent to plan in advance. Nevertheless, looking at the target too long may distract the agent, potentially impeding its performance. To address this challenge, we introduce two solutions. Firstly, we propose a module called the emotion regulator to look past the target at a distance, promoting long-term planning and improving the agent's emotional resilience. Secondly, we introduce a module called the conscience, which looks back at past experiences, enabling the agent to learn from past mistakes and learn more quickly. Together, these regulation mechanisms enable the VAEAM model to learn more robust policies, as demonstrated by the model's superior performance in the Gymnast, Fetch, InvertedPendulum, and HalfCheetah algorithms when compared to the baseline VAEAM.

If dark matter is composed of subatomic particles, it's likely that they reside in compact states, especially if they interact via a force carried by a massive particle. Because of this state, their behavior as wave-like entities is negligible. In this study, dark matter with short-range interactions is examined to see its potential for forming compact lumps. It is found that, depending on the specific parameters, dark matter could exist in two compact states - one with a density peak at the center, resembling a fermionic state, and another with uniform density, resembling a bosonic state. Furthermore, it was determined that the characteristics of the peak density, especially its size and height, can be calculated with a reasonable degree of accuracy, and that its consistency with the observed density of the local galaxy is also feasible. In a particular scenario, it's possible for dark matter to exist in compact, planet-like bodies, and these predictions are verified using the constraints imposed by the "missing satellite problem" from galaxy formation. Additionally, it's forecasted that the unique internal structure of these compact dark matter states could be identified by their gravitational influence on a passing galaxy.

In this study, we establish a connection to Cerebellar neurobiology to drive our Cerebroid model and utilize its properties to enhance our training methodology. First, we model the forward loop of the Cerebellum as a computational framework, which leads us to develop an innovative approach for optimizing training and achieving higher accuracy from the start. Additionally, we enhance our method by incorporating a form of annealing based on the complex neurobiological process involving Purkinje neurons and Elf2, enabling a more gradual decrease in our method's randomness. Furthermore, we demonstrate how our method can be successfully applied to a broad range of cognitive tasks, the details of which are presented in the supplementary information on our Github repository.

Researchers have developed novel approaches to studying finite-dimensional nilpotent algebras from multiple perspectives, including commutative and anticommutative cases. By nilpotency index four, these algebras can be described using a single pair of vectors in a d-dimensional space. The researchers focus on categorifying such geometric families using stratified categories with linear invariants, employing methods from the theory of quadratic algebras and their representations, as well as spin representations of orthogonal Lie algebras.

Early-time active galactic nuclei (AGNs) form in the first billion years of the universe, with the most massive black holes emerging from supermassive black hole formation. These black holes develop powerful jets of particles and radiation, which can regulate their growth through interaction with surrounding infalling gas. This process is influenced by the cosmic microwave background radiation's effect on the gas's development. Our simulation, which spans from 800 to 1200 million years in the past, reveals that jet development is affected by two types of CMB-recoil forces: one that is symmetric and the other is skewed towards the prior jet direction. This implies that observations of the most distant jets may provide insights into the accretion processes of the black holes. Nevertheless, the characteristics of the jets remain largely unaffected for the observer.

A broad class of symmetric rank-2 tensor Lagrangians is constructed in terms of the曲率 two-form, completing a classification for classical gravity in any number of dimensions with arbitrary symmetry, whether geometric or not. It's noted that these Lagrangians correspond to generic diffeomorphism invariant theories of the gravitational field.

We have developed an approach to register image sets by combining local and global descriptors, specifically adapting SIFT features representing local information and using the Symmetry Points symmetry descriptors, known as SP-Symmetry, for global descriptors. After extracting features from set A, we compute descriptors for each individual image within the set, then select one representative image based on consensus, extracting its dominant symmetry points and associated contours. These descriptors are subsequently used to register a selected reference image, chosen either manually or through an automated process that picks the set with highest content overlap with A. We've assessed our method through experiments on animal brain scans from different species, achieving effective registration of brains of a mouse and a rat, and successfully matching anatomical features such as the ventricles and external surfaces. We've made the ordinal optimization code available on GitHub.

The discovery of an intriguing binary star system, SDSS J082239.54+304857.19, was first reported in 2018, where it was determined to be the sixth known type of binary white dwarf star with varying brightness, exhibiting a 40.5-minute interval eclipsing pattern.  Using data from numerous sources, this study further analyzes the characteristics of this unique system through various methods, utilizing measurements from 2014 to 2021.  By employing different mathematical expressions and taking into account factors such as color changes, distortion, and irregularities, this research provides insight into the properties of both components, their masses, radii, and temperature.  Additionally, this study estimates the distance from the Galactic plane and velocity of the system.  Using temperature values, this study calculates the rate at which momentum is transferred in the system due to gravitational wave emissions, determining a 3.4x10^-11 s^-1 binary decay frequency.  Further calculations indicate that within the next 3.1 million years, the binary will undergo three successive phases of shrinking orbit, merging into a singular object.  Finally, this study makes recommendations for using the system as a template for modeling similar binary star systems, and suggests that it could be an ideal candidate for further observation with advanced telescopes like the JWST.

Recent research has focused on developing methods to compare and summarize time series or spatially based data. Global aggregation, which seeks to find a representative summary that minimizes average distances to the original datasets, has emerged as a prominent approach for this purpose. A key challenge in this field is identifying an appropriate distance metric. Although the Euclidean distance is commonly used for time series data, it corresponds to an ideal transport distance in the context of global aggregation. This distance metric allows cases where no perfect representative exists, resulting in representative summaries that are suboptimal. This discrepancy highlights the need for novel measures of similarity between the original data and the representative summaries. To address this, this study proposes a new distance metric for evaluating time series, which accounts for time shifts. By combining this distance metric with a time warping function, we can redefine the optimal representative and calculate a distance between the original data and the representative summary. This distance is then used to assess the quality of the representative, which is typically assessed by the residual time series. A crucial component of this approach is generalizing the time warping function, which we achieve by leveraging the concept of an time series distribution and defining the time warping function as the mapping corresponding to the conditional distribution of one component given another.

We examined galaxies associated with different types of active galactic nuclei (AGN) in the redshift range of 0.1 to 0.5 using data from the 2df and GAMA surveys. Our analysis focused on the spatial distribution and morphological characteristics of these AGN host galaxies. We observed that star-forming AGN tend to be hosted in less dense regions compared to radiative AGN, which have no such preference. Furthermore, star-forming AGN display a moderate tendency to align within their host galaxies, whereas radiative AGN show no notable alignment pattern. These findings suggest a potential disparity in the impact of environmental factors on these AGN types.

This paper investigates four-dimensional Lie groups that admit a flat rotational plane field with a pointwise 1-type Gaussian map. It is  stateD that such groups either is isomorphic to a standard four-dimensional torus or one of several non-abelian groups, including those with a structured basis and specific structural constants.

Neural networks perform superior task solutions when utilizing prior knowledge of data, which can be acquired through various approaches such as pre-training on numerous images or introducing numerous regularization terms during the training phase. In this research, we investigate whether learning depth information from a single camera is an effective approach for providing prior knowledge for a segmentation network, which we find to be an improvement over training on pre-existing large-scale image datasets. Additionally, we introduce a novel depth assessment approach that achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Depth AI Challenge benchmark, demonstrating its new benchmark status. The experiment results indicate that our proposed depth assessment models serve as an optimal choice for pre-training segmentation networks for various applications.

Time-series data is increasingly essential across various fields, yet a deep understanding of its contents is vital for effective decision-making. To bridge the gap between raw data and insights, recent studies have explored neural storytelling, aiming to create comprehensive narratives from time-series data. However, most models are tailored to specific domains (like medicine) or require extensive manual input to generate stories. To address this limitation, we propose TCube, a novel transformer-based model capable of generating domain-applicable neural stories through the analysis of general temporal patterns. TCube's approach involves creating story embeddings that capture the underlying story information, allowing it to learn the story vocabulary and temporal patterns through self-supervised training. Evaluation under different evaluation protocols showcases TCube's ability to generate stories across various domains without any domain-specific training, as well as its superior performance on the NumBAM story evaluation task.

The ATLAS collaboration at the Large Hadron Collider has conducted comprehensive studies into the realm of particle physics, specifically focusing on the delicate balance of CP symmetry and rare occurrences in beauty meson interactions. Our report provides a comprehensive overview of recent studies undertaken by the ATLAS team, covering processes that challenge our understanding of conservation laws and beautiful meson behaviors. The findings presented here have been presented at scientific conferences in 2018 and 2019, including CPEPPC 2018 and CWG-Flav 2019.

On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising ferromagnetic model and identify novel periodic measures weakly periodic with period 2, for which the periodic critical values are calculated. The existence and unique existence of such measures are examined based on specific functional relationships between the magnetic field and temperature. The relationship between the first Lyapunov number of a specific functional equation and these critical values is also explored.

A specific type of hyperbolic Cauchy problem with variable, sublogarithmic coefficients is studied, representing an extension of previous research on log-Hölder bounded coefficients. A new class of function spaces, suitable for this class of problems, is introduced, and their properties are investigated in detail. A novel introduction to the concept of well-posedness for categories of hyperbolic problems in the sense of N. S. Landau is presented, and it is proven that the introduced space class includes a wide range of other spaces previously studied for similar problems, making them well-posed under the new framework. Furthermore, the main findings of the article position the research on hyperbolic problems with sublogarithmic coefficients as direct generalizations of studies on their bounded log-Hölder counterparts.

The process of breaking down Japanese text into meaningful units, such as words, phrases, or names, depends on accurate term segmentation. Increasing the granularity of segmentation can improve search results and other natural language processing tasks. Recent advancements utilize Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks to handle long-range dependencies in Japanese term segmentation. This paper proposes a simplified version of the model, known as Extended Short-Term Memory (ESM), that effectively captures short-term memory in Japanese term segmentation without the need for complex directional operations found in LSTM. Experiments conducted on the CUED dataset and NIST Open Domain dataset demonstrate that the proposed model achieves competitive results with state-of-the-art models, such as Bi-LSTM and Bi-ESN. Notably, the model outperforms Bi-LSTM and performs on par with Bi-ESN across multiple evaluation metrics, such as F1-score and accuracy, across various granularities of Japanese term segmentation.

On Stack Overflow, developers seek assistance with programming issues they encounter,
resulting in a substantial portion of the community posting helpful code snippets
in the 'External Links' section of questions, despite existing restrictions
imposed by site policies. This study examines posts with external links shared
on Stack Overflow to identify frequent sources of these links. We present an
automated link extraction method and show that links found in 'External Links'
are distinct from those discovered through other examination methods. To ensure
compliance with Stack Overflow's guidelines, developers should refrain from
posting external links in comments; an alternative would be for them to report
useful code snippets found online on the site's meta platform, allowing the community to maintain a collective library of shared external connections.

Recent findings from the DESI galaxy survey have brought up a potential issue, where the density of galaxies appears to be higher in directions aligned with the North Pole of the Cosmic Radio Source, a phenomenon that could be linked to the axion-like particle anomaly. New data from the Planck CMB survey has not fully resolved this tension. In this study, the researchers have calculated the full probabilities for eight different models attempting to resolve the galaxy distribution discrepancy. Their analysis revealed that only one model is consistent with all available data, which is the model incorporating large-scale magnetic fields to influence the galaxy distribution, with a confidence level of 69%.

Effective climate communication is crucial due to the significant challenges in conveying critical climate information. Although various methods have been explored to overcome these challenges, effective communication has so far been limited to providing individuals with personalized and timely weather forecasts. To address this, researchers have developed a Climate Information Repository that leverages powerful data analysis and cloud technology to make climate data more accessible and easier to understand. This Climate Repository integrates information from multiple sources, including personal preferences, local patterns, ideal scenarios, and the characteristics of effective climate communication, to empower individual climate communicators with real-time access to a vast database of climate information.

Domain generalization is essential for NLP models applied in clinical settings, considering the irregular formatting and variable writing styles of medical notes. We introduce the Sign Event Extraction (SignEE) problem, requiring models to identify cardiovascular and gastrointestinal-related symptoms in medical notes with different languages, reflecting real-world clinical encounters in Asia. In this study, we explore the possibilities of implicit domain generalization through text obfuscation, employing explicit and masked anonymization methods. The masked approach demonstrates superior performance on previously unseen datasets from China and Singapore, validating the concept. Furthermore, the findings on SignEE contribute to the understanding of event extraction and clinical NLP.

Profound RL is a novel AI system designed for self-driving cars, using a combination of deep learning techniques and reinforcement learning rewards to create a more intelligent and adaptable driving intelligence module. Profound RL's unique approach leverages transfer learning and reward shaping based on the vehicle's state and action components to generate more intelligent driving behaviors. When tested in various driving scenarios, Profound RL demonstrated the ability to transfer training from one environment to another, producing consistent and reliable results. Furthermore, Profound RL exhibited superior capabilities in handling complex situations, such as automatic vehicle lane changing, by outperforming existing AI systems in terms of success rate and stability.

A problem in neural network applications, known as categorization, has limited its applicability due to its high computational cost in embedded systems. Categorical neural networks are employed to tackle this issue, yet they are often ineffective due to poor performance and complex designs that hinder implementation. This study presents an advanced Spiking Categorical Neural Network (SCNN) inspired by the human brain's categorization abilities, which accurately reflects its structure and function. The proposed SCNN, with its novel spike inhibition layer, incorporates a dual spike memory system, derived from biological categorization processes, to retain crucial information. Furthermore, we have created a dual-layered learning algorithm that efficiently propagates errors, enabling faster convergence. Our research thoroughly compares SCNN with traditional artificial neural networks in terms of accuracy, computational load, hardware feasibility, and biological plausibility. Experimental results demonstrate that SCNN, with its enhanced performance, low computational burden, and implemented hardware costs 50% less than its artificial counterpart, outperforms existing spiking categorical models.

The internal composition of Strange Quark Stars is complex and poorly understood. 
Researchers have found that extremely strong magnetic fields within these stars can significantly alter their properties. 
This study investigates the impact of finite temperatures and magnetic fields on the structure of spin-aligned Strange Quark Stars, 
using the mean field approximation to analyze the up and down quark mass generated by Wang et al. 
It's discovered that the generated mass is minimal, 
and that the results align well with those obtained through lattice QCD for constant mass u-quarks and v-quarks in the presence of M. 
When the quark mass increases, the radius of the spin-aligned Strange Quark Stars decreases, 
and the masses remain unchanged as the magnetic field's direction shifts from parallel to anti-parallel. 
Additionally, the U-shaped density profiles of the magnetic field components within the star are distinct from the electric charge density, 
which displays an increasing one-dimensional profile similar to that of baryon density. 
Unitless causal equations of state are generated, 
revealing that the mass and radius of these stars are largely unaffected by finite temperatures and opposing magnetic fields.

Pando is a calendar-based distributed computing framework that enables individuals to voluntarily run processes in their web browsers on demand, without requiring a dedicated account or installation. It achieves this by utilizing the built-in web storage systems, specifically workers and storage, in modern web browsers. To protect the user's privacy and ensure their consent, Pando's design incorporates a demand-based model, a verification process, and the division of the computing population into small, manageable groups. We implemented Pando using a unique approach to account and storage management, as well as a web-based interface for visualizing the computing groups and analyzing data. We evaluated Pando's effectiveness through a proof-of-concept implementation, as it successfully balances the needs of scientists, who want to maximize the size of the computing group, with the needs of volunteers, who want to control who they're helping.

The solution to numerous advanced scientific issues can be formulated as a nonlinear eigenvalue problem on the spectrum $\sigma$ with the general equation $A\tau + \tau^\dagger B\tau + C\sigma = 0$. However, solving this equation directly is often impractical due to its high dimension, particularly in applications like computing the natural frequencies or modes of structures. Therefore, researchers have developed various approximation techniques for the equation and typically aim to find isolated points on the spectrum. A novel and efficient algorithm has been created to estimate nonlinear eigenissues using the RIE method and the Galerkin projection technique for solving the resulting equations. This estimation technique also incorporates numerical methods for computing the singular values and singular vectors of matrices in solving nonlinear eigenvalue problems. This technique allows for calculating not only the location of eigenissues but also their associated modal issues in addition to providing information on the stability of isolated eigenissues. A comparison was carried out on several test cases to validate the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed technique.

The $\beta$-transitions introduced by Regev, Shor, and Wulcan in 2019 serve as an extension of Konyev's $\beta$-transfers, effectively covering all greedy transitions at certain split points in the $\beta$-expansion of 1. The proposed "intermediate $\beta$-transitions" modify the $\beta$-transitions by allowing a certain degree of greediness deviation, thus narrowing the gap between them. The new intermediate transitions maintain key properties, including preservation of $[0,1)$ and the Lebesgue measure, and will be compared with previously proposed "bad $\beta$-transitions" introduced by the second author in 2019.

We analyze equidimensional dilute diagrams in $SO(N_c)$ and $Sp(N_c)$ gauge theories with $N_f$ Majorana fermion doublets and $N_f$ $SO(N_c)$ or $Sp(N_f)$ vector-like fermions, focusing on their lower dimensionality aspects. For $SO(N_c)$ theories, these diagrams consist of two sections, and in the first, diagrammatic arguments are used to demonstrate that the $O(4N_f - 4)$ chiral symmetry of this diagram is broken. The second diagram, representing a confined phase of the theory, displays an $O(4N_f) \times Sp(N_c)$ chiral symmetry breaking. The lattice simulations for $SO(3)$ and $Sp(2)$ theories, consisting of 2 flavors of Majorana fermions, verified the disruptions in chiral symmetry in both confined phases. The simulations also showed the absence of $N_f$ $U(1)_V$ baryon number symmetries. The simulations on an $8^4$ lattice for a $Sp(2)$ theory, consisting of 2 flavors of fermions, also showed the mass gap of the theory.

Machine learning models, such as random forests, are popular choices for classification and regression due to their accuracy, but their predictability is compromised by complexity. This study introduces assignments and discretization curves as new concepts to analyze feature importance in tree ensembles. The assignments indicate optimal feature values for minimizing loss, while discretization curves show the impact of restricting feature values to the assignments. Region importance, defined as the minimum loss within a discretized region, is introduced as a new metric to replace permutation importance. This new metric avoids the bias of underestimating the effect of large-scale continuous features found in ensemble models. The introduced tools, assignments and discretization curves, are useful for understanding and enhancing tree ensemble predictions, allowing users to make informed decisions about which feature values to target for improving predictions. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated with real-world datasets including mortgage, kidney, mortgage, and house prices.

Machine Learning (ML) models are becoming increasingly central to various sectors, but the data training and model inference often involve sensitive information that's at risk of breach. To address this concern, researchers have been exploring the capabilities of hardware-based security features, particularly Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs), to safeguard confidential data and models. One significant challenge arises from the limitation of a single server with TEEs to process training data, which can easily be compromised. This paper addresses the problem by proposing Flatee, a TEE-centric federated learning framework that integrates the security of hardware with the principles of federated learning to minimize data movement outside of clients' control, thereby minimizing trust requirements and enhancing overall security. Flatee leverages software and hardware features, such as Remote Procedure Calls (RPCs) attestation, to verify the integrity and trustworthiness of computational resources, enabling secure model aggregation and inference within a network of clients without the need for a trusted aggregator. Instead, Flatee's design leverages a decentralized approach to federated learning, where each client acts as a secure aggregator, and model aggregation takes place within a network of clients without data leaving the clients' control, and no outside TEE is involved. Furthermore, Flatee's design leverages the principles of zero-trust architecture to ensure the security of the ML model training and inference processes, and provides the first step towards fully hardware-secured federated learning, with implications for the development of secure and privacy-preserving ML models

The increasing reliance on automated and autonomous vehicles must be complemented by robust solutions for compact footprint integrated systems that streamline operator interaction and vehicle monitoring, yet current approaches leave significant room for improvement in this area. An interactive vehicle behavior monitoring and performance evaluation system has been developed to facilitate efficient operator performance assessment within small integrated vehicles. The proposed solution employs a dual-camera setup for comprehensive interaction monitoring, with data processed in real-time using a single-board computer based on the Linux environment. The performance evaluation algorithm, running on a dedicated embedded graphical interface with a compact user-friendly design, allows for real-time monitoring, time-based reporting, and real-time adjustments to the algorithm, while also facilitating off-line analysis with high-quality video captured from the integration. The developed solutions have found practical applications in various automated and autonomous integrated vehicles, including a self-driving forklift, a teleoperated mobile robot, and a human-cargo automated guided vehicle.

The security of applications derived from containerized microservices is increasingly significant, given their widespread use across various industries. These services are highly specialized, making it difficult even for top security experts to devise effective safeguards, let alone the average developer. In response to this challenge, automated security verification methods for system call restrictions are emerging, yet they fall short in tackling all relevant system calls, particularly those not visible within the application code. To address this gap, we introduce Timeloops, an innovative method for automatically discovering system call patterns both inside and outside of application codes for system call rule learning. Timeloops ensures that distinct execution paths are examined by pairing unique system call sequences with corresponding runtime intervals. These internal and external execution paths are identified by comparing current and subsequent interval timings. We demonstrate Timeloops' efficacy by applying it to the task of security rule validation, yielding a significant increase in rule count and coverage, especially for internal execution paths, by over three times and ten times respectively. Furthermore, our research reveals that Timeloops can successfully recover critical system calls that are often missed by conventional approaches, resulting in a substantial enhancement of security rules.

Research into item representation using factorization-based methods for linear classifiers has gained attention, particularly in understanding their computational efficiency. Our investigation delves into the conditions under which linear classifiers in the latent space correspond to margin-based classifiers, a property that indicates a separation between support vectors and data points. We discover that this condition holds for logistic regression but not necessarily for perceptron. Furthermore, through visual analysis of two-dimensional data, we identify a geometric relationship between the classifier and the data, providing insight into the classifier's behavior.

This research analyzes the distribution and composition of stars within the Milky Way's nuclear bulge, centered on the supermassive black hole Sagittarius A*, using two decades of adaptive optics observations from Keck. By applying a segregation framework to the K-band luminosity function, we identified three distinct populations: a massive stellar population, a low-mass stellar population, and a young stellar population near Sgr A*. We confirmed the presence of stellar segregation, with the low-mass population exhibiting smaller dispersion in line-of-sight velocity and radius from Sgr A* compared to the overall nuclear bulge. However, when factoring in the line-of-sight velocity distribution, we found that the massive and low-mass populations exhibit similar dispersion, with both's velocity distribution centered at approximately 100 parsecs. Our study also revealed that the low-mass population's line-of-sital velocity dispersion is consistent with predictions from N-body simulations of a massive black hole system, whose observed properties align with those of M31's globular cluster systems. Additionally, we discovered that the low-mass population's size may exceed previous estimates due to previously unrecognized distant members, whereas the massive population is likely confined to the region within the Large Binary Epicenter radius.

We analyze a regulation mechanism implemented through simulation, utilizing model predictive control and a stochastic process. The simulation instance draws inspiration from the OSNAP project's work on predictive network control. The model involves multiple agents, each managing a resource with dynamic capacity. A central planner randomly assigns orders for these resources. Each agent follows a pursuit-regression trajectory based on its current state and the target level set by the planner. This iterative process continues until convergence or the expiration of a predefined timer.

The primary objective of this research is to establish the theoretical basis and establish frameworks for identifying and comprehending the inherent connections between a manifold and its high-dimensional projections through compressed observations. Under the assumptions of compressive sampling and the independent component model, where a low-dimensional data source is independently projected into orthogonal, non-Gaussian distributions within a high-dimensional space, we are capable of recovering the underlying geometry and structure of the source manifold. This study extends existing compressed linear regression methods for parameter estimation and develops novel algorithms for recovering the intrinsic connections and structure of the source manifold from these compressed observations. The proposed methods employ intrinsic component analysis and technique such as principal curve and its non-parametric version, while addressing the challenges posed by the independent component model and the compressive sampling process. The proposed framework is demonstrated to be effective and efficient, particularly with the support of the RIP, a concept used in the field of compressed sensing. The framework is particularly relevant to the field of high-dimensional data analysis and understanding the inherent structures within complex datasets.

A cellular automaton model, based on the dynamics of two competing species, was examined on percolation networks derived from the ERG and IC lattices. The model takes into account both inter-species competition within a species' own territory and colonization in unoccupied sites. At a certain threshold of competition intensity, one species' ability to colonize adjacent empty sites is restricted, leading to the extinction of that species and coexistence within the remaining threshold, with the outcome determined by the relative strengths of the two species' competition-colonization balances. Notably, this model, dynamic in nature, displays a form of coexistence that contrasts significantly with the phase separation observed in static species competition systems, exhibiting complex dynamics that may offer inspiration for understanding coexistence patterns in nature.

We establish a set of equivalent conditions for von Neumann algebras in abelian quantum dual models to exhibit a property known as finiteness. The main condition is the presence of a non-zero, positive, invariant region. Furthermore, the contravariant dual of a region equivalent to the zero region is strictly convex. We define a categorical structure, consisting of morphisms as inclusion maps of equivalent equivalent regions, and prove it to possess the properties of a management system of equivalent algebras.

Our proposed approach implements a loop of coherent feedback connecting the magnon, phonon, and photon systems within the magnomechanical system. We demonstrate the generation of multipartite entanglement among these three subsystems by applying the feedback from the magnon to the phonon and photon, based on the linear magnon-photon-phonon interaction. Furthermore, our findings show that the feedback circuit can enhance and stabilize the entanglement between the magnon and phonon sectors, as evidenced by increased logarithmic negativity and residual entanglement.

In a specific framework used to handle divergities in quantum field theories, new operator equations are derived that isolate and factor out the complex triple-collinear behavior present in loop diagrams. These equations, applicable to QCD and using a particular regularization method, provide a way to systematically separate this behavior, an important component in developing subtraction schemes used to isolate infinities in next-to-next-to-leading order calculations. The approach offers an alternative to traditional approaches, offering advantages in clarity and efficiency. The method is then extended to include the next-order interaction in the alpha-squared calculations, involving new, regularized terms and updating key operator equations with these additional components.

A formal proof for the Neron Desingularization in one-dimensional local domains has been formulated, and it was originally attributed to Gruson and Raynaud in 1979. Later, an alternative construction was offered by Temkin, though his work drew upon the initial studies of Gruson and Raynaud. In this mathematical context, we consider a one-dimensional local domain $(R, M)$ and aim to find a sequence of maps, beginning with a local complete intersection $(R_n, M_n) \to (R, M)$, where each $R_n$ can be expressed as $R[x_1, \dots, x_{2n}] / I_n$ with $I_n$ being an ideal generated by $n$ elements in $x_1, \dots, x_{2n}$. The proposed construction relies on two key tools: Valuations and Blowups, with the former used to develop a version of the Valuation Criterion, allowing for the selection of appropriate centers for Blowups in order to achieve the required results.

The Indonesian archipelago's vast sundial collections are an essential component of the local educational institutions and historical sites. Unfortunately, public understanding of these important astronomical instruments is inadequate. Historically, the principles of using sundials to tell time and navigate were integral to the knowledge systems developed by the ancient Javanese people. In earlier times, it was common knowledge how to construct sundials and utilize them effectively. However, the educational systems of the last century or so have not emphasized the practical applications of astronomy and celestial navigation as they should. Although scientific literacy is a priority in the curriculum, the focus has shifted away from traditional methods of timekeeping and navigation that rely on simple tools like sundials. This research article, "Suryakala - Nusantara", introduces a new initiative to revive the study of sundials and explore the creative possibilities they offer. We will discuss our experiences in documenting and preserving the historical sundials in Indonesia, as well as presenting our creative explorations with them.

This correspondence explores a next-generation integrated data and power transmission network with D2D comms capabilities that features a RIS助力 system to enhance overall performance in a dark matter dimension. The overall system efficiency, measured by the difference between the D2D transmission power and the harvested power, is optimized by jointly adjusting RIS助力 system. The resulting non-convex problem is broken down into sub-problems that are solved using different methods such as block coordinate descent, successive convex approximation, and lambda-mu dual methods. The efficiency of the proposed approach is validated through numerical analysis, and it is shown that RIS助力系统 effectively improves overall system efficiency and power harvesting levels while minimizing D2D transmission power.

Achieving precise control of a single-point LDV system is crucial for obtaining accurate measurements in flow diagnostics experiments. The difficulty in regulating the system increases with its distance from the operator, which can be mitigated by utilizing an offset borescope and an automated tracking algorithm. The tracking method employs feedback based on the offset borescope's video signal to dynamically adjust the Single Point LDV's position in the plane perpendicular to the flow direction. The effectiveness of this approach was demonstrated in obtaining a two-dimensional velocity field from a free-shear flow. The system's offset borescope, tracking algorithm, and related software have been developed in-house and can be utilized for flow diagnostics studies.

In a detailed exploration, the concepts of eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and especially the idea of first-order spectra for graphs with unidirectional connections are introduced and illustrated with concrete examples.

A new device called a programmable phase disk (PPD) has been introduced to modify wavefront distortions in transmission electron microscopes (TEMs). Typically, wavefront irregularities in TEMs are addressed using a dedicated aberration corrector with dedicated coils, resulting in reduced image contrast and blurred features. The PPD offers a flexible alternative by attaching to the TEM's condenser lens system and modulating the electron wavefront in real-time using a flexible film with an electron-refractive pattern. This novel approach enables the correction of wave irregularities while providing a flexible phase disk aberration corrector with its own merits.

The house edge in gambling represents the average percentage of gambled money that is expected to be retained by the house, acting as a measure of advantage for the house, but not, in a statistical sense, an accurate estimate of winnings. When the total amount gambled is denoted as T and the house edge is E, the expected income for the house is EA, yet this does not accurately predict the house's actual earnings. Instead, one can anticipate the house either profiting or losing the amount: (x + 1)^2 + (a - 1)^2 + b, where x represents the amount of money the house would need to not go bankrupt. Furthermore, a separate calculation, suitable for implementation in spreadsheet software like Excel or Google Sheets, has been established to calculate net profits in scenarios where the house edge is guaranteed, as long as the total gambled amount exceeds this figure.

This paper counts the positions reachable by a random walk of length $2n$ in $d$-dimensional space, starting from the origin and remaining within the set of integer coordinate points whose coordinate sum's absolute value equals $k$. The proposed method involves summing the coefficients of a specially constructed polynomial, yielding a closed-form expression with up to $d+1$ terms, significantly simplifying the original expression with up to $d!$ terms.

This paper delves into the detailed spatial structure of the Gambini-Olmedo-Pullin (GOP) model of black holes within the framework of loop quantum gravity. It's through this expanded model that we can restore the local Lorentz invariance, which had been compromised in previous models. To better understand the black hole's spatial geometry, we compute and visualize the proper distance and cross-sectional area functions, which reveal that GP models remove singularities by also creating a region of infinite extension, in addition to the wormhole region. Furthermore, our findings show that any GP model with non-zero polymer parameters can be matched with the higher-dimensional Schwarzschild black hole solutions. In addition, we investigate the impact of these parameters on the black hole's quasinormal frequencies of varying masses.

Our research focuses on thermal properties of graphene and transition-metal dichalcogenides, specifically how they affect heat transfer between electromagnetic fields and the environment. We investigate this further in doped graphene, considering the impact of thermal populations on electromagnetic fields within the environment at finite temperatures. For the first time, our study FRET experiments on isolated, thermally equilibrium, doped graphene panels have验证了 thermal polarization fluctuations, as predicted by our theoretical model through solving the Kubo-Greenwood formula, considering electromagnetic interactions in all directions. Moreover, our findings reveal that the thermal equilibrium property possesses a unique characteristic, distinguishing it from zero-temperature correlations, leading to differences in heat transfer when the environment is not in thermal equilibrium.

Improving speech generation beyond current models that consider only the speech history is crucial, as they produce low-quality speech with limited accuracy and unintelligible speech at high speeds. A proposed method, MaskedSpeech, uses a masking approach to incorporate the entire speech context, enabling the model to access both past and future speech. The framework also includes a novel two-stage training strategy with a high-quality text-to-speech model and a high-performance speech-to-speech model. Additionally, Low-Rank Adaptation techniques are employed to reduce the speech decoder's training difficulty and data requirements. Demonstrations and evaluations confirm MaskedSpeech's superior performance in speech quality, accuracy, and formant matching.

Bayesian models are known to be highly accurate, but their complex integrations are computationally expensive, leading to slower analysis and potentially impractical run times for large datasets. Breakthroughs in variational inference have managed to accelerate these integrations, yet it has been difficult to match its results with those from Markov chain Monte Carlo and previous methods like Markov chain Monte Carlo and nested sampling, which serve as gold standards. This research presents the use of space mapping to create a quicker, more efficient variational model, and we test its effectiveness on both real-world and previously studied problems, showing that it can produce accurate results at a significantly reduced cost.

Although deep learning models have achieved remarkable success, they have also been found to have a critical weakness where maliciously altered input can bypass the classification systems. This issue has led researchers to investigate how adversarial examples can be created, particularly in deep learning models, and how it can be utilized to expose vulnerabilities. This paper focuses on two central questions: (1) can adversarial examples be generated using deceptive generative models without prior knowledge of the target classification system, and (2) can these adversarial examples be utilized to mislead a target classification model through the manipulation of an intermediary? Our initial findings demonstrate that generative models can be employed to create adversarial examples for classes they were not trained on. Furthermore, these adversarial examples can be generated in a way that causes a misclassification by a target classification model without the aid of post-processing. However, experimental results reveal that the transferability of these adversarial examples is relatively low.

Climate change misinformation is a pressing issue within the realm, with conspiracy theories surrounding the global warming narrative posing a particularly challenging obstacle. Despite numerous studies examining various forms of climate misinformation, research specifically focusing on climate change conspiracy theories has been relatively limited. This study identifies and categorifies the most prevalent climate change conspiracy theories as shared and discussed on social media platforms, with particular emphasis on Facebook. By analyzing actual conversations among users, this study discovers that eight prominent conspiracy theories are frequently debated online, with "Climate Extortion" being the most prevalent. Furthermore, the study observes that the discursive structures surrounding these conspiracy theories vary significantly, with some relying on personal testimonials and others on statistical data to convey their respective messages.

Researchers have investigated the potential for dark matter and a single top quark, or two top quarks, to be produced together within proton-proton proton collisions at the LHC with a 13 TeV energy level. Using the CMS dataset, collected at 2016, at 35.9 fb^-1 energy, they employed the STopS model to simulate the interaction of dark matter and top quarks. To determine the cross-sectional areas of these reactions, they set the transverse momentum of the top quarks at 50 GeV. Following the simulation, they created and displayed standard model predictions on control top quark events, utilizing the matrix element method. Their analysis revealed an upper limit on the cross-sectional area of 0.42 pb at 95% confidence levels, which in turn yielded a constraint on the mass of the dark matter at 4.5 GeV.

Given an n-exangulated framework with exact n-sequences established, we prove that it satisfies Auslander-Reiten-Serre duality, and this duality is equivalent to specific conditions. Additionally, in the context of exact sequences in n-exangulated categories, we demonstrate the duality and its equivalence to certain conditions. Building on this duality, we also define and characterize stable equivalence of n-exangulated categories with respect to tilting n-exangulated subcategories. Furthermore, we provide examples that illustrate specific properties, including but not limited to: (1) non-isomorphism between the endomorphism rings of two tilting subcategories despite stable equivalence, and (2) non-isomorphism between the endomorphism rings of two tilting subcategories within the same n-exangulated category, which are stable equivalent.
